future.title: Progress and challenges towards eliminating vertical transmission of HIV in India - Scientific Reports
future.content: Download PDF ## Abstract India has intensified efforts towards elimination of vertical transmission of HIV (EVTH) as part of National AIDS and STD Control Programme-V (NACP-V). We present the progress in achieving NACP-V’s EVTH goal as of year 2023-24. We analysed the 2023 state level data using Spectrum model in 2023 to measure the coverage of anti-retroviral treatment among pregnant women, annual paediatric HIV case incidence rate and final vertical transmission rate. UNAIDS and WHO definitions for these indicators were used. In 2023, around 2350 new paediatric infections were estimated by vertical transmission. However, 44% of these transmissions resulted from incident HIV infections among pregnant and breastfeeding women. Overall, paediatric HIV incidence per 100,000 live births decreased from 25.2 (14.7–46.6) in 2019 to 10.4 (6.1–19.3) in 2023. During the same reference period, final vertical transmission rate (inclusive of breastfeeding period) decreased from 25.28% (17.06–37.99) in 2019 to 11.75% (7.93–17.66) in 2023. The 2023 India HIV estimates, using recent data and global modelling tools, highlighted progress in eliminating vertical transmission of HIV. Early identification of HIV-positive mothers and starting them on lifelong ART is crucial. Additionally, generating local evidence is needed on interventions like safe practices, repeat testing, and feeding practices to inform policy decisions. ### Similar content being viewed by others Article Open access 06 April 2023 Article Open access 22 November 2021 Article Open access 19 November 2021 ### Subjects * Health policy * HIV infections ## Introduction In the early 2000 s, evidence demonstrated that administering antiretroviral (ARV) medications to women living with HIV during their pregnancy and breastfeeding can reduce the vertical HIV transmission rates to under 5%1,2,3,4. As a result, UNAIDS and WHO identified elimination of vertical transmission of HIV (EVTH) as a public health priority in 20095,6. Since then, substantial global guidelines for concerted actions have emerged with specific indicators to measure the attainment of EVTH7,8,9,10. This encompassed achieving impact indicators, including an annual paediatric HIV incidence of less than 50 per 100,000 live births and a final vertical (both perinatal and postnatal) HIV transmission rate under 5% in breastfeeding population (or 95%) with final vertical transmission rate of 10% (8–13%)11. Till September 2024, 18 countries have received World Health Organization (WHO) validation certificate for EVTH12. Use of models like Spectrum is an accepted approach to assess progress on vertical transmission indicators10,11. Spectrum, developed by Avenir Health (www.avenirhealth.org) in collaboration with UN agencies like WHO and UNAIDS, is a user-friendly suite of policy models that equips user with a robust analytical tool to inform decision-making and support evidence-based planning. The tool is used for estimating the demographic ramifications of the HIV/AIDS pandemic, encompasses the AIDS Impact Model (AIM) module, which simulates the complex interplay between demographic, epidemiological, and programmatic factors influencing the trajectory of the HIV epidemic. By integrating a myriad of data inputs, including antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage, mother-to-child transmission probabilities, and mortality rates, AIM generates a nuanced and multifaceted portrait of the epidemic’s impact on population dynamics, including that of vertical transmission rates, thereby informing the development of evidence-based policy interventions, resource allocation strategies, and service delivery modalities. India, with around 2.54 million people living with HIV (PLHIV), is home to the second largest number of PLHIV across the globe11. Government of India is implementing the National AIDS and STD Control Programme (NACP) since 1992 driven by evidence-led, evolving, and comprehensive response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic13. Specific interventions for prevention of parents to child transmission (PPTCT) under NACP were initiated during phase-2 (1999–2007) of the programme. Single dose Nevirapine (sdNVP) was the cornerstone of the PPTCT programme under NACP till 2011 (NACP-3). In 2012, when NACP-IV was initiated, triple-drug ARV regimens throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding (Option B) were introduced. The strategy was further modified in 2013 with a policy of initiation and life-long retention on triple ARVs as soon as pregnant women were diagnosed with HIV infection14. The initial goal was to achieve the elimination of vertical HIV transmission by 2015, but this target year was later moved to 2020. NACP adopted dual elimination of vertical transmission of HIV and syphilis as a priority area in its strategic plan for the period of 2017-2415. In 2020-21, around 23 million HIV tests were done among pregnant women in India against an estimated 30 million pregnant women in the country. In the same year, against the estimated size of nearly 21,000 HIV positive pregnant women requiring services for prevention of vertical transmission of HIV, around 11,000 were put on life-long ARVs and an overall vertical transmission rate of more than 20% was estimated16,17. NACP phase V, launched to anchor the national AIDS and STD response for the five-year period of 2021-22 to 2025-26, focused on elimination of vertical transmission of HIV as one of the five high-level goals to fast-track the progress. By increasing coverage of HIV testing among pregnant women and getting every HIV positive pregnant woman initiated and retained on ARVs in collaboration with the public health systems as well as the private sector, the goal focussed on attaining elimination of vertical transmission in alignment with WHO recommendations by 2025-2618. In this paper, we present the progress made towards attainment of this third goal of NACP-V until the year 2023-24, which is the third year of implementation of the NACP-V. The objective is to analyse the trends of impact indicators of paediatric HIV incidence per 100,000 live births and final vertical HIV transmission rate as per WHO recommended targets for elimination using the State-wise Spectrum models for the 2023 round of estimates. ## Methods Both HIV surveillance and HIV burden estimation are institutionalised annual activities under the NACP that provide up-to-date information on the magnitude and direction of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the country and its constituent states as well as union territories19,20. This activity is done by formally engaging government institutes and indicators pertaining to prevalence, incidence, mortality, and vertical transmission of HIV by State and Union Territory are annually estimated. The Spectrum mathematical model, developed by Avenir Health, UNAIDS, and partners, is utilised for this purpose. ### HIV burden Estimation using spectrum model Globally, 170 countries use the Spectrum modelling tool to assess the impact of HIV on their populations. This tool is regularly updated to account for the latest scientific evidence on demographics, programme impact, fertility, mortality and incidence under guidance and direction of the UNAIDS Reference Group on Estimates, Modelling and Projections. The procedures and methodology are discussed in detail elsewhere21,22. In essence, Spectrum models are based on demography, treatment coverage, and HIV prevalence data to generate HIV incidence estimates and trends by age, sex, and CD4 + counts. The dynamic nature of the model permits transitioning of newly infected individuals over time with change in age, CD4 + count, and treatment (or non-treatment) categories. Typically, the Spectrum output is estimation of the PLHIV population by age and sex every year. Adjusted fertility rates are applied to Women living with HIV (WLHIV) aged 15–49 to estimate HIV-positive mothers requiring ARV treatment to achieve elimination of vertical transmission. Adjusted fertility rates for WLHIV account for the influence of HIV infection on fertility23,24. The model subsequently estimates the vertical transmission rate by considering the type and coverage of ARV treatment alongside the probability of vertical transmission by type and duration of ARV coverage during the perinatal and breastfeeding phases25,26. ### HIV estimates 2023 under NACP of India In India, disease burden is estimated annually using State/Union Territory (UT)-specific models, except for the union territory of Lakshadweep, which lacks surveillance data. The UTs of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are modelled together since Ladakh currently does not have sufficient surveillance data to be independently assessed. For performing HIV Estimates 2023, Spectrum 6.33 version was employed. Each model was set-up for the period of 1981 to 2036. The Spectrum modelling tool typically sets the start year five years prior to the first reported case of local HIV transmission. Consistent with this approach, the State/UT model in India initializes simulations in 1981, projecting forward to 2036. This extended timeframe enables policymakers to forecast the potential magnitude and trajectory of the epidemic beyond the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, facilitating proactive planning and strategic decision-making to address the evolving needs of the HIV response. State models for the 2022 round of estimates were updated with the India and State-specific latest data on ARV coverage and HIV prevalence generated through routine programme monitoring, surveillance surveys and national family health survey data. Default parameters were retained only when India or State-specific evidence on that parameter was not available. All of the models were aggregated using the ‘Aggregate’ function of the Spectrum to produce the national estimates. HIV Estimates 2023 was done through a tiered institutional arrangement comprising working and review by Technical Subgroup (HIV Burden Estimation), Technical Working Group (Surveillance & Epidemiology) and Technical Resource Group (Surveillance & Epidemiology). ### Programme coverage update Work up for HIV Estimates 2023 required updating of programme coverage data on elimination of vertical transmission of HIV (EVTH) and ARV (Adult and Paediatric) till 2023 in each State model, using the NACP programme monitoring data (Table 1). At the national level, the aggregated number of pregnant women receiving ARVs for eliminating vertical transmission was around 17,700; the highest in the country since the launch of the programme (Fig. 1). **Table 1 State/UT-wise HIV-positive mothers receiving PPTCT, 2005–2023.** Full size table **Fig. 1** Full size image Number of pregnant WLHIV on anti-retroviral prophylaxis/treatment coverage. On-ART retention among HIV-positive women at delivery was updated to 97% for those on ART before pregnancy and 94% for those detected during pregnancy; although Spectrum’s default values were 85% and 80%, respectively. This was done after undertaking an analysis of on-ART retention data at the time of delivery among HIV-positive pregnant women registered at the ART centers under programme. The analysis was undertaken separately for newly detected pregnant women and those already on-ART when becoming pregnant. Nationally, a total of 10,130 HIV-positive women were already on-ART before current pregnancy while 7641 were initiated on ART during current pregnancy. Data on breastfeeding practices were also updated in 2023 round based on the programme data. For the 2023 round, breastfeeding practices for HIV-positive mothers who were not on-ARVs was kept as same as that of a non-HIV infected pregnant woman from the findings of the National Family Health Surveys (NFHS). This was done under an assumption that WLHIV who were not on-ARVs were not aware of their HIV status, and the breastfeeding practices among them might be the same as those reported by NFHS for all mothers. For HIV-positive mothers who were on-ARVs, programme data analysis revealed a lower proportion of HIV-exposed babies receiving breastfeeding in each age group vis-à-vis all mothers (Fig. 2). The inputted data on feeding practices for HIV-positive mothers on ARVs were updated accordingly by accounting for this difference. **Fig. 2** Full size image Percentage of mothers doing breastfeeding by babies age-group. ### Fertility adjustments and vertical transmission patterns update In each State/UT-model, data on total fertility rate and age-specific fertility rate were inputted based on the Sample Registration System (Registrar Government of India). The inputted fertility data were adjusted to account for the influence of HIV infection on fertility. The Default Spectrum values for age-specific fertility adjustments for HIV + women on and off ART were retained (Supplementary Table 1) in the absence of India-specific data on the same. The ‘Fit local adjustment factor’ button in Spectrum was used to best fit the fertility reduction value to data on prevalence among pregnant women. Spectrum had provisioned this feature to improve the match to prevalence among pregnant women and the estimated PMTCT coverage. The probability of vertical transmission of HIV depends on the stage of infection of the mother, the duration of breastfeeding and the ARV regimen. The default rates in Spectrum were not changed (Supplementary Table 2). ### Prevalence data updates Epidemic configuration for each State/UT model was set-up as concentrated epidemic. Under this pattern, 15–49 yrs population in each State/UT model was distributed among five populations subgroups viz. female sex workers (FSW), men who have sex with men (MSM), hijra/transgender (H/TG) persons, people who inject drugs (PWID), and general population. For the population subgroups of FSW, MSM, H/TG and PWID, the prevalence data was updated till the year 2023 based on the HIV prevalence data from sentinel surveillance and positivity data among these populations from routine testing under the programme. For the general population, the epidemic data was updated till 2023 using the HIV sentinel surveillance data and routine testing data among pregnant women. Data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-3 and NFHS-4) were also inputted to inform the HIV epidemic curve in the general population. ### Epidemic curve fitting and calibration ‘Spectrum’ offers various modelling options, including *Estimation and Projection Package (EPP) Classic* and *R-Hybrid*, for generating epidemic curves. The recommendation is to use *EPP Classic* in scenarios where prevalence data is limited while to use *R-Hybrid* when multiple years of prevalence data from multiple sites are available. HIV burden estimations under NACP use the *EPP Classic* and *R-Hybrid* models. EPP Classic uses four parameters: time of epidemic start (t-zero), the proportion of the susceptible population at risk of HIV infection (f-zero) at t-zero, transmission rate for untreated adults (r), and behavior change rate. R-Hybrid combines two different models of the transmission rate: one for the initial stages of the epidemic and another for more recent trends. Until the 2000 s, the R-hybrid model utilized a four-parameter logistic function to represent the transmission rate: log of the initial epidemic growth rate, log endemic transmission rate after the epidemic has stabilized, rate of decline of the log transmission rate as the epidemic stabilizes, and time of the inflection point of the logistic function. From the mid-2000s, when HIV epidemics are considered to have stabilized to a state of endemic transmission dynamics, the model used a piecewise-linear spline with a first-order random-walk (RW1) penalty on the spline coefficients to model changes in log r(t). The piecewise-linear spline allows the transmission rate to vary with recent epidemic trends, whereas the RW1 penalty assumes that the expected transmission rate remains steady with linearly increasing variance. For the general population, R-Hybrid model was used to do the epidemic curve fittings for all States with at least 10 surveillance sites among pregnant women. Among the rest, EPP classic model was used to do epidemic curve fittings for the general population. For rest of the population groups, EPP classic curve fittings was used. During curve fittings, prevalence conditions were applied to remove the unrealistic curves in line with UNAIDS recommendations27. The Spectrum modelling process advises applying prevalence conditions to exclude unrealistic scenarios when default randomly generated curves contradict expert opinion or epidemiological evidence. For example, if curves depict implausibly rapid and high epidemics inconsistent with a country’s epidemiological record, a constraint such as ‘prevalence in 1985 must be less than 5%’ can be applied. Following this approach, state/UT-specific prevalence conditions in 2023 round were applied based on local knowledge and evidence. HIV burden estimate process in India calibrates the epidemic curve generated through EPP Classic/R-hybrid using the data from probability-based survey in community settings to account for inherent biases in facility-based surveillance28,30. The curve fitting and calibration method used in the Spectrum modelling tool is detailed elsewhere31,35. EPP is calibrated using a Bayesian approach namely Incremental Mixture Importance Sampling (IMIS). IMIS identifies points with high importance weights in areas where the target density is underrepresented. Each iteration adds a multivariate normal distribution centered at the highest weight point to the importance sampling distribution, forming a mixture with the prior. This process iteratively improves representation of underrepresented parameter space, creating an importance sampling distribution that accurately covers the target distribution. Further, the model calculates a calibration constant to account for the difference between the surveillance-fitted prevalence and the observed prevalence from population survey. This constant is applied to each prevalence trajectory, and then re-sampling of scaled trajectories is done to generated adjust epidemic curves in alignment with representative surveys prevalence. This approach allows for the incorporation of population survey data into the model, enabling more accurate estimates of HIV prevalence. In 2023 round, the calibration on general population was not applied for 4 states, viz., Arunachal Pradesh, Tripura, Punjab, and Rajasthan. This was done because applying calibration was leading to a PLHIV size estimates which was lower than the actual number of PLHIV currently under the programme. In the next step, the sex ratios and incidence rate ratios were updated according to the epidemic type (Concentrated non-IDU or Concentrated IDU pattern) within Spectrum’s ‘sex/age pattern’ Table36. ### Uncertainty analysis and aggregation Uncertainty analysis represents the concluding phase in updating a State model. This was accomplished using the ‘Uncertainty analysis’ tool within Spectrum. The tool produces plausible range of estimates for critical epidemiological outputs by conducting 1000 Monte Carlo iterations. These iterations take into considerations uncertainties in adult incidence along with uncertainties around other essential assumptions such as fertility, incidence, and mortality, based on global or regional data. Spectrum’s default values for mean and standard deviation on uncertainty variables were applied in absence of India-specific data. The national estimates were generated by aggregating the State model using the “Aggregate” tool of Spectrum. ### Description of indicators used in results We present the analysis of outputs generated through the HIV Estimations 2023 model at State and national level on the indicators of EVTH-service coverage, paediatric HIV incidence rate and vertical HIV transmission rate. The descriptions of the presented indicators are given below36. 1. a. HIV-positive mothers in need of ARVs for prevention of vertical transmission: The number of HIV-positive women giving birth each year and, therefore, in need of ARVs to prevent HIV transmission to the baby. 2. b. % HIV-positive mothers initiated on ARV: The percentage of HIV-positive mothers needing ARVs who are receiving it in that year. 3. c. New paediatric infections due to vertical transmission: The number of children who become infected due to vertical transmission in a year. This includes perinatal transmission and up to 36 months of breastfeeding. 4. d. Vertical transmission rate at 6 weeks: The percentage of babies born to HIV + mothers who are infected by 6 weeks of age. 5. e. Final vertical transmission rate including breastfeeding period (%): The percentage of children born to HIV + mothers who will eventually be infected due to vertical transmission at current transmission rates. This includes perinatal transmission and up to 36 months of breastfeeding. 6. f. Vertical transmission by source: Disaggregation of new vertical infections by timing (prenatal or during breastfeeding) and ARV (on an off) regimen. ### Ethics statement HIV surveillance and estimation was an ongoing activity under NACP done through a robust institutional arrangement. Prior to each round, the institutes presented their methodology and ethical considerations to their ethics committees for approval. Data collection under the surveillance survey was undertaken upon receiving local ethics committee approval. Institute ethics committee of All India Institute of Medical Sciences (India, New Delhi) approved the ethical considerations for the 2023 round of HSS vide reference no IEC-629/15.07.2022 dated 15.07.2022. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant operational guidelines and ethical considerations approved by the Ethical Committee. Data collection in surveillance was done as per the approved method after obtained written informed consents from selected respondents. HIV burden estimation was carried out through the institutional arrangements by utilising aggregated, de-identified data following each round of HIV surveillance. ## Results Nationally, 19,962 (16,403 − 24,737) HIV-positive mothers were in need of ARVs for prevention of vertical transmission (Table 2). Overall coverage for ARVs in HIV-positive mothers in 2023 was 89.02% (71.96 - >=95) with a vertical transmission rate of 5.06% (2.98–8.47) at 6 weeks and final transmission rate (including breastfeeding period) of 11.75% (7.93–17.66). Overall, 2339 (1372–4344) new vertical HIV infections were estimated among children of which around 44% were from women who acquired incident HIV infections either during pregnancy (8%) or breastfeeding (36%) (Fig. 3). Another 22% were from women who did not receive ARVs during pregnancy. 12% of estimated vertical transmission were among HIV-positive mothers who didn’t receive ARV during breastfeeding; 8% were among HIV-positive mothers who dropped off from ARV during pregnancy; while another 5% were among mothers who dropped off from ARV during breastfeeding. **Table 2 National-level results on EVTH. 2019–2023.** Full size table **Fig. 3** Full size image Distribution of total estimated vertical transmission in 2023 by timing of infections and ART status, India. Two States, Maharashtra, and Uttar Pradesh had 2000 or more HIV-positive pregnant women in need of ARVs for prevention of vertical transmission. Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Karnataka, Punjab and Telangana had HIV-positive mothers in the range of 1000–2000. Three States/UTs (Sikkim, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, and Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu) had 10 or less HIV-positive mothers (Table 3). **Table 3 State/UT-wise results on EVTH (2023).** Full size table In eight States/UTs (Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, and West Bengal) ARV coverage among HIV-positive mothers was 95% or more. Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Odisha, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and Telangana had ARV coverage rate of HIV-positive mothers of 90% or more. Seven States/UTs, (Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, Manipur, Sikkim, Tripura, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, and Puducherry) had coverage of less than 75% in 2023. Fifteen States/UTs (Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Assam, Chandigarh, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, Kerala, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal) had paediatric HIV incidence per 100,000 live births of 10 or less. Two States, Mizoram and Nagaland, had paediatric HIV incidence of more than 100 while in Manipur, it was more than 50. Meghalaya, Punjab and Tripura were the other States/UTs where paediatric HIV incidence per 100,000 live births was in the range of 40 - = 30% was noted in States/UTs of Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Tripura and Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu. In Nine States/UTs (Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, Goa, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, Puducherry, and Arunachal Pradesh), less than 10 children were estimated to get HIV infection on account of vertical transmission. In thirteen States (Assam, Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Haryana, Meghalaya, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram Punjab, Rajasthan, Tripura, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal), more than 40% of vertical transmission were from mothers who were estimated to have had incident infections during breastfeeding period (Fig. 4). These States also had 7-15% of the vertical paediatric infections from mothers who have had incident infections during pregnancy. In Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Kerala, Manipur, Nagaland, Tamil Nadu and Uttarakhand, at least 25% of the vertical transmission were from mothers who did not receive ARV during pregnancy. In Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Manipur, Nagaland, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, and Uttarakhand, at least 10% of the vertical transmission were from mothers who did not receive ART during breastfeeding. In Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and West Bengal, at least 10% of vertical transmission were from mothers who dropped off ARV during pregnancy. **Fig. 4** Full size image State/UT-wise distribution of total estimated vertical transmission in 2023 by timing of infections and ART status, India. ## Discussion Eliminating vertical transmission of HIV is central to India’s commitment of ending AIDS epidemic as a public health threat by 2030. The NACP-V (2021-22 to 2025-26) aims for, *inter alia*, an annual paediatric HIV incidence below 50 per 100,000 live births and a vertical HIV transmission rate under 5% by 2025-2618. We measured State/UT-wise progress on these impact indicators up to 2023-24. Although an enormous progress has been observed nationally, a very diverse and complex scenario unfolded sub-nationally thereby underlining the need for tailored strategies. As NACP-V intensifies focus on elimination of vertical HIV transmission by adopting it as one of the five top level goals, there is a dramatic progress on related impact indicators. Paediatric HIV incidence per 100,000 live births decreased from 25.2 in 2019 to 10.4 in 2023 while final vertical transmission rate (including breastfeeding period) decreased from 25.28% in 2019 to 11.75% in 2023. Progress on impact indicators targets had been accompanied by significant increase in ARV coverage among WLHIV for EVTH which increased from 60.42% in 2019 to 89.02% in 2023. This had been most evident in the States of Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Madhya Pradesh where the final vertical transmission was very near to the target level of 5%. In these States ARV coverage among HIV positive mothers was more than 90%. Overall, around 2350 new paediatric vertical infections were estimated to happen in 2023; almost 59% lower than the estimate for 2019. A significant proportion (44%) of these vertical transmissions resulted from women with incident HIV infections, either during pregnancy or during breastfeeding period. In States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Punjab, and Tripura, at least 60% of the total vertical infections were from women who had incident HIV infections. These were States where overall HIV incidence rate was higher than the national average37. Incident HIV among pregnant and breastfeeding women, coupled with the significant risk of vertical transmission, poses a well-documented challenge to achieving the elimination of vertical transmission of HIV38,39,40,41. Vertical transmission likelihood is as high as 18% among newly infected pregnant women. If the maternal HIV infection occurs during breastfeeding, the probability of vertical transmission can rise to 27%25,26. Couple counselling that encourages safe behaviours, greater involvement of male partners in adopting safe sexual practices during pregnancy and breastfeeding, including pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), have been recommended in various contexts to prevent new HIV infections among women42,43,44,45,46. The WHO recommends repeat HIV testing to ensure early diagnosis of new HIV cases during pregnancy and breastfeeding47. This recommendation has been incorporated into the national HIV testing guidelines for EVTH-related services in many countries48. Studies in diverse settings, including in India, have demonstrated repeat HIV testing as a cost-effective strategy for EVTH49,50. Implementation research for testing the strategies for primary prevention for HIV infections among pregnant and breastfeeding women, as well as early identification of incident infections, at least in States/UTs where HIV incidence rate is high, will be critical for India’s progress on EVTH. Around 21% of the total 2350 new paediatric vertical infections in 2023 in India occurred during breastfeeding period from mothers who had a HIV infection prior to the last delivery. HIV transmission through breastfeeding is well documented51,52,53,54. In Spectrum modelling tool (v6.33), based on experts’ review, transmission probabilities among non-incident HIV-positive breastfeeding women was set in the range of 0.51-0.89% per month for off-ART mothers and in the range of 0.02-0.20% per month for on-ART mothers depending upon CD4 count and duration of treatment25,26. The probability of HIV transmission through breastfeeding poses a significant policy challenge. Breastfeeding is promoted globally, including in India, for its essential role in reducing infant mortality and under-five mortalities through optimal nutrition, protection against infections, and aiding in child spacing55,56,57,58. The risk of HIV transmission through breastfeeding versus the high morbidity and mortality-risk without it has led to evolving guidelines on feeding practices for exposed infants. This included endorsing decision of replacement feeding, in 2001, by mothers under proper counselling supporting settings where it is acceptable, feasible, affordable, sustainable, and safe (AFASS)51,52,53,,55,56,57,,59. WHO current guidelines recommend that country health authorities decide if HIV-infected mothers should either breastfeed with antiretrovirals or avoid breastfeeding60,61,62. In countries promoting breastfeeding, HIV-positive mothers should breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue up to 24 months or longer while being on lifelong ART. The Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have recommended that women who are HIV-positive should not breastfeed to reduce perinatal HIV transmission in the United States63,64. Impact of infant feedings choices vary by country context. Replacement feeding, together with lifelong ART have been positively associated with significant gains in prevention of vertical transmission, especially in high-income countries, and have been included in intervention packages by countries65,66,67,68,69. However, evidence has also indicated that the reductions in HIV transmission achieved through replacement feeding can be counterbalanced by increases in HIV-unrelated morbidities and mortalities, particularly in developing countries70,71,72,73. Economic and social contexts of replacement feeding have further compromised health outcomes for mothers and exposed babies59,74,75. Replacement feeding is linked to significantly reduced rates of vertical transmission. Nevertheless, it is essential to generate evidence specific to India to ascertain whether the advantages of replacement feeding outweigh the risks of non-HIV morbidity and mortality associated with the lack of breastfeeding for HIV-exposed infants. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have emerged as priority states to achieve elimination goals in the country. Uttar Pradesh had a population of approximately 233 million, while Bihar’s population is around 125 million76. These states also had the highest total fertility rates, at 3.0 in Bihar and 2.7 in Uttar Pradesh. Due to their large population size and high fertility rates, these two states accounted for nearly 20% of the total EVTH-service needs in the country. While the coverage of EVTH-services in Uttar Pradesh was about 92%, it stands at approximately 55% in Bihar, with the final vertical transmission rate reaching 29%. More than half of the vertical transmissions in Bihar were estimated to occur among children whose mothers did not receive ARV treatment during pregnancy or delivery. Uptake of antenatal care services in Bihar was low, only 68% of the mothers reported receipt of antenatal care for their last birth from a health professional while one-fifth reported not receiving any antenatal care services77. Sustained focus on augmenting family planning, antenatal care, HIV testing and ART initiation in collaboration with routine maternal, and child health services would be the key to making progress on vertical transmission in such States69,78. Repeat HIV tests in the third trimester, during labour, and/or while breastfeeding can significantly aid progress by identifying mothers who have recently contracted HIV, allowing them to join long-term HIV care and start ART42,43,44,45,46,47,48,49,50. Equally important will be focus on Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Sikkim, Tripura, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, and Puducherry as the final transmission rate in these States/UT in amongst the highest in the country. Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh have a rising HIV incidence which further underlines the need for urgent attention. Other States with rising HIV incidence (Punjab, Assam, and Meghalaya) will also augment their progress on EVTH with concerted efforts for interventions among pregnant and recently delivered women. ### Limitations Estimating vertical transmission using the Spectrum modelling tool involves specific limitations, which have been previously mentioned in the context of HIV vertical transmission estimation in India21,26,79,80. The 2023 India HIV Estimates utilized State/UT-specific data on input parameters such as coverage, retention, and breastfeeding patterns for HIV-positive women covered in the programme. However, the data on fertility adjustments and vertical transmission probabilities employed default values provided within the model. Many of these defaults’ values are based on studies coming from foreign settings which may or may not be applicable for Indian context36. Conducting a nationally representative study to update the parameters pertaining to HIV impact on fertility and vertical transmission probabilities will be important for NACP. Another limitation of this study is that the outputs of the Spectrum model were not validated against empirical data. Programme data from paediatric HIV diagnoses and ART initiations could be used to validate the model’s estimates of vertical transmission. A consistency across States in the ratio of number of paediatric HIV diagnoses to the modelled number of vertical transmissions would provide insights into modelled estimates. If that ratio isn’t stable, it could point to problems with the programme data, problems with the model assumptions, or both. Currently, this validation by using programme data cannot be undertaken for three primary reasons. Firstly, the detection of HIV-positive pregnant women under the programme against the estimated need is not uniform. Secondly, the testing of HIV-positive exposed infants at 6 weeks, 6 months and 18 months under the programme against the reported live-births vary significantly inter-State. Thirdly, data reported under the early infant diagnosis programme refers to the number of tests conducted, rather than the number of infants who received the tests, which hampers the correct understanding of vertical transmission rate from the programmatic data. Future efforts to strengthen the cohort-based longitudinal data reporting could enhance the feasibility of using available data sources to validate the model’s outputs and refine its assumptions. Future progress monitoring on EVTH goal would benefit from conducting sensitivity analyses. Such analyses would allow for the exploration of how variations in model parameters, assumptions, and data sources impact the estimated outcomes. By undertaking sensitivity analyses, there can be better understanding of the potential sources of uncertainty and identify areas where further data collection or refinement of model parameters is warranted. This would ultimately enhance the reliability and generalizability of estimation results, providing policymakers and stakeholders with more accurate and informative evidence to guide decision-making. The Spectrum modelling tool defines vertical transmission rate as the percentage of children born to HIV + mothers who will eventually be infected due to vertical transmission at current transmission rates. However, mothers who seroconvert during breastfeeding are not included in the denominator. Ideally, they should be. For India, the estimated vertical transmission rate is 11.75% (2339 transmissions out of 19,962). However, if we include the estimated 2911 mothers who seroconvert during breastfeeding in the denominator, the rate drops to 10.23% (2339 transmissions out of 22,873). Given the importance of accurate vertical transmission rates, it’s essential to include mothers who seroconvert during breastfeeding in the denominator. ## Conclusion India HIV estimates 2023 utilized the latest version of globally recommended modelling tool and incorporated the most recent State/UT-specific data on demographics, programme coverage, and prevalence. The study highlighted significant progress made towards eliminating vertical transmission of HIV. However, there is no room for complacency. Traditional interventions, such as early identification of HIV-positive mothers and initiating them on life-long ART, remain essential to eliminating vertical transmission of HIV in India. Generating local evidence on the effectiveness of interventions, such as adoption of safe practices, repeat testing during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and feeding practices, will inform policy formulation for prevention and detection of incident infections. Future research exploring regional patterns and their correlates with socioeconomic factors will enable policy deliberations and actions improving healthcare outcomes. ## Data availability Main data is provided within the manuscript or supplementary information files. India As the HIV epidemic enters its fifth decade, India recorded more than 1.7 million new cases of HIV in the last 10 years between 2011 and 2021.1 As per the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO), the year 2021 witnessed around 62,967 new HIV infections.2 The new HIV infections in India has declined by nearly 90 percent since hitting the peak in 1997. This was possible due to evidence-based and result-oriented strategies and program interventions of NACO and partners. However, there is need to further accelerate this response to attain India's commitment to achieve the United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) 95-95-95 targets by 2030 and end the AIDS epidemic as a public health threat by 2030 in line with Sustainable Development Goals. To attain the UNAIDS 95-95-95, i.e., 95% of those living with HIV to know their status, 95% of those who know their status to be on treatment and 95% of those on treatment to be virally suppressed, India needs to strengthen the prevention-testing-treatment-care continuum.3 Prior to introduction of HIV self-testing (HIVST) approach, reaching the "first 95" was primarily through testing strategies, like facility-based testing, community-based testing, index-testing, social network testing and partner testing. About HIV self-testing HIVST is a screening test, which is performed often in a private setting, either alone or with someone the person trusts, by using oral fluid or whole blood as specimen. It is an innovative approach, which is recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) to diversify and amplify existing HIV interventions.4 More than 50 countries across the world have adopted HIVST as one of their testing strategies for increasing testing coverage and thus knowledge of one's HIV status. The global HIVST policies have been informed by several studies. Evidence from various studies has not only shown that HIVST is feasible, acceptable and effective among various populations but has also highlighted that it is safe and easy to administer with minimal support. A few studies conducted in India also observed that HIVST is highly acceptable to key populations (KPs) and recommended it to be introduced for them.5,6 Furthermore, there is also evidence that HIVST has rarely been misused or has caused social harms that could be associated with its use. However, to further strengthen the evidence, and to guide the implementation plan for HIVST in the Indian context, this demonstration project was proposed and implemented. About STAR HIV self-testing project in India The Unitaid-funded STAR HIV Self-Testing Initiative is an initiative to generate evidence for decision-making, enabling environment and catalyzing the global market for HIVST. The first phase in Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe generated vital information on effective, ethical and efficient distribution of HIVST products and answering questions about the feasibility, acceptability and impact of this intervention. The second phase expanded the evidence generation on HIVST to three additional African countries - South Africa, Lesotho, and Eswatini (formerly Swaziland). Built on the lessons learned and evidence from previous two phases of HIV STAR Initiatives in Africa for HIVST, the third phase of the project was implemented in India, in addition to six other countries, to understand and address the barriers to roll out of HIVST and 5 provide evidence of developing structures and systems for long term sustainability of HIVST in the country. The third phase of STAR HIVST project was a multi-centric project implemented by PATH, with the support of UNITAID through Population Service International (PSI), across 50 districts from 14 states of India (Figure 1). Beginning in February 2020, the Unitaid-funded STAR HIV Self- Testing Initiative had three desired outputs –  Output 1: Enabling environment created to support introduction of HIVST, including policy adoption and product registration.  Output 2: Service delivery models implemented that increase the potential of uptake of HIVST and linkages to care, treatment and prevention services.  Output 3: Dissemination of best practices from HIVST implementation at the country-level, and identification and mobilization of resources to support transition and scale-up of HIVST. The project aimed to demonstrate the feasibility and acceptability of HIVST among different KP groups and other high-risk groups to generate evidence to inform an HIVST policy in India. More specifically, the project aimed to –  Assess the feasibility, acceptability, and demand for HIVST across specific population and models.  Assess the preference for blood- or oral fluid–based HIVST kits and approaches (assisted and unassisted).  Assess linkages to prevention services for those with negative HIVST results; and to confirmatory HIV testing and treatment services for those with HIV reactive results.  Identify the challenges to the linkages and any social harm following HIVST. Figure 1. The states of India where the STAR HIV self-testing project was implemented 6 HIV self-test kits When the initial landscaping for HIV self-test kits was done by PATH for the project, it was discovered that there were no Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) approved HIVST kits in India. The project used HIVST kits manufactured by three manufacturers and pre- qualified by WHO, namely the oral fluid–based OraQuick® and blood based INSTI® and Mylan® through various delivery models. An import license was obtained from the Drug Controller of India (DCGI) to import and use these kits in the country for the STAR HIVST project. Partners in the HIV STAR project This project was implemented by PATH through Humsafar Trust (Alpana Dange as the Principal Investigator), Solidarity and Action Against The HIV Infection in India (SAATHII), International Training & Education Centre for Health Private Limited (I-TECH), Voluntary Health Services (VHS), Society for Health Allied Research Education (SHARE India), National Coalition of PLHIVin India (NCPI+) and International Labor Organization (ILO), WHO, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)-National AIDS Research Institute (ICMR-NARI), and ICMR-National Institute of Epidemiology (ICMR-NIE) as technical partner with the support of NACO, Ministry of Health, Government of India. Additionally, the project was supported by more than 200 community-based organizations (CBOs) and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across the country. 7 Key initiatives to achieve the desired outputs Initiatives to build an enabling environment for introducing HIV self-testing Prior to this project, HIVST was an unchartered territory in India. Although evidence-based testing strategy, implementation of HIVST has its own challenge, such as acceptability of self- tests, individuals’ willingness to pay for them, ability to reach individuals not accessing conventional HIV testing, pre-test counselling, post-test counselling, and linkage to care. For the intervention to be successfully piloted in India, close working with NACO and its state counterparts, i.e., the State AIDS Control Societies (SACS) and CBOs, was required. The project also required to have the confidence of the regulatory bodies, such as the CDSCO, as well as Department of Health Research (DHR) to validate the purpose, objectives, and approaches of the intervention, as there were no approvd HIVST test kits in the country at the time of the project. The project further required the support of HIVST kit manufacturers, for them to make their kits/essential documents available for research by the project. PATH India HIV Self Testing Project Advisory Group (PISPAG): PATH constituted an advisory group, the PISPAG, which had representation from NACO, SACS, development partners, UN Agencies, ICMR institutions, academic institutions, and technical experts. The seven core implementing partners of the project, i.e., PATH, Humsafar Trust, SAATHII, ITECH, ILO, SHARE India, and NCPI, also participated in the PISPAG. The PISPAG played a key role as the project's advisory body providing guidance, insights, and solutions to critical issues during the conceptualization and implementation. Jointly chaired by the former Health Secretary to the Government of India, former Special Advisor to UNAIDS, and former Special Envoy to the Secretary of the United Nations on HIV/AIDS for the Asia Pacific region, Dr. JVR Prasada Rao, and former Additional Director General, Central Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, Dr. Ashok Kumar, the PISPAG also functioned as an interlocutor between the project, policymakers, and played a key role in the processes that were essential for integration of HIVST into HIV testing in the country. Community Advisory Board (CAB) for HIV self-testing: The CAB was a body of representatives from all key population groups and PLHIV and was the voice of the community to the project. Engaged deeply with the project, the CAB looked at the community processes and practices adopted by the project and ensured that they are community sensitive and community inclusive. The CAB consisted of 18 members, invited by name and representing four KPs – Persons Who Inject Drugs (PWID), Female Sex Workers (FSW), Men who have sex with men (MSM) and Transgender/Hijra population (TG/H) – in addition to PLHIV. The chair of CAB, unlike that of PISPAG, was rotational. The PISPAG and the CAB were national level bodies constituted by PATH for guiding the project. They met regularly, virtually due to the COVID-19 related disruptions during the project period, but never jointly. PATH ensured that the proceedings and decisions of PISPAG were shared with CAB when they met and vice versa. State Oversight Committee (SOC) for HIV self-testing: Besides engaging the stakeholders at the national level, the project also engaged key stakeholders from the SACS, District AIDS Prevention and Control Units (DAPCUs) and representatives of KP and PLHIV communities at 8 the state level through the SOC for HIVST. The project had one SOC for HIVST in each of its 14 intervention states. SOC for HIVST was a collaboration between the government, PLHIV, and community-led organizations from affected communities, as they worked jointly to facilitate more inclusive decision-making on issues that are important to members of KP and PLHIVs. Adopting a transparent, consistent, and multi-channel communication approach, it contributed to building trust among all those involved, including government, service providers, community groups and sponsors. Community Monitoring Board (CMB) for HIV self-testing: Understanding and acknowledging the importance of strengthening local decision-making, educating communities, and enhancing community capacity and effective community engagement for HIVST, the Community Monitoring Board (CMB) was formed at the district level for the STAR HIVST project. Comprising of leaders and vocal members from the key communities and selected by representatives of the field implementing partners (CBOs/NGOs), the CMB acted as a focal point to address the grievances of the project participants. The chair of the CMB was chosen by consensus of all members of the CMB, on a rotational basis. Involving HIVST kit manufacturers: When the project was being conceptualized, HIVST kits were not manufactured indigenously in India. There were three WHO PQ HIVST kits available globally but only one of them had a distributor in India. The HIVST kit manufacturers required regulatory approval and test license from DCGI. PATH facilitated the consultations between local distributors and HIVST kit manufacturers, so that they can present their clinical trial protocols to DCGI for regulatory approval. As a result, the two HIVST manufacturers were able to establish local distributorship, an essential pre-condition for receiving test license from DCGI. At the time of writing this report, there were seven HIVST kit manufacturers who had received DCGI test license and one of them had received clinical evaluation protocol approval. PATH supported the manufacturers by reviewing their clinical evaluation protocols and providing them with feedback. From no interest in introducing HIVST in India to seven HIVST manufacturers, and more approaching DCGI for regulatory approval and test license, the landscape of HIVST manufacturers in India witnessed a complete turn-around. Engaging regulatory bodies: The project obtained approval from multiple regulatory bodies as it took shape of a research project. PATH received approvals from five different regulatory bodies, before starting the HIVST pilot. PATH, through Fermish Clinical Technologies Private Limited, received DCGI Subject Expert Committee approval to conduct the field implementation of the project for HIVST kit under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act 1940 and Devices Rules-2017. The approval came with active advisory input of ICMR and NACO. The DCGI approved the use of WHO pre-qualified HIV self-test kits – INSTI HIV Self-Test, OraQuick® HIV Self-Test and Mylan HIV Self-Test – for the project, which was archived in the Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI), hosted at the ICMR's National Institute of Medical Statistics and functioning under the Health Ministry’s Screening Committee (HMSC) for conducting the clinical trials for HIVST. The Institutional Review Board of Humsafar Trust provided the project ethical approval for the study. The engagement of CDC and the United States President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) partners in India further required the clinical evaluation protocols for HIVST to be subject to their Office of Scientific Integrity. CDC facilitated their approval. 9 Development partners: In addition to the partnerships with CBOs and organizations representing key communities, the project also partnered with NACO's Targeted Interventions partners, ILO's workplace intervention partners, Global Fund partners, and PEPFAR partners through CDC. By the start of field implementation phase of this project, PATH had created an ecosystem where all stakeholders – national, state and district level government bodies; organizations representing KPs at the national, state and district levels; HIVST kit manufacturers; regulatory bodies; and development partners – were aligned for exploring HIVST as a solution to enhance HIV testing capacities in the country. Initiatives to increase the potential of uptake of HIVST and linkages to care, treatment, and prevention services From August to October 2021, PATH conducted a formative study to explore enablers and barriers driving demand of HIVST among high-risk groups, and the feasibility and scalability of implementing HIVST in India. Using human-centered design (HCD) thinking, the qualitative study found that there is an opportunity for HIVST to reduce stigma by minimizing the duration of interactions associated with HIV, in addition to reducing the inconvenience and opportunity cost of getting an HIV test. It also highlighted that there were perceived fears of making an error while conducting a self-test and questions around the credibility of seemingly an over-simplistic product for a deadly disease, besides drawing comparisons with confirmatory tests conducted at ICTCs. Service delivery models for HIVST To address these concerns and find the opportunities to enhance the feasibility, acceptability, and demand for HIVST across KPs, PATH, in consultation with members of PISPAG and CAB, identified five different distribution models:  Community-based model  Private practitioners’ model  Workplace model  PLHIV network-led model  Virtual model The intent of the studying the five models of distribution of HIVST kits shared below was not to assess the comparative advantage of one model over the other, but to independently assess the feasibility and acceptability of each of the five models. Furthermore, these models are also non- comparable as each of them were designed to reach different population groups. Model#1: Community-based model: This model was implemented with CBO partners and was designed to reach FSWs, MSMs, TG/H and PwIDs. Along with these, this model also aimed to reach the partners and clients of these KP groups and other self-identified high-risk groups. In this model, trained peer volunteers from the KP community conducted demand generation activities. Trained peer counsellors did the eligibility assessment, pre-test counselling, demonstration of HIVST through the use of videos and other job aids to help participants make an informed choice about their preferred HIVST kit – either oral or blood based and the preferred testing approach – assisted or unassisted. HIVST kits were provided to the project staff through the participating CBOs. Based on the result of the HIVST, the CBO followed the algorithm for post-test counselling, confirmatory test (for those who had reactive or indeterminate results with HIVST) and prevention, treatment, and care support as per the national testing guidelines. This 10 model was implemented across 50 districts in 14 states with Humsafar Trust, SAATHII, ITECH, and VHS as the lead implementing partners and around 250 field implementing CBOs. Model#2: Private provider model: The second distribution model implemented with private providers, who were regularly providing services to patients with sexually transmitted infections (STI) and their partners, chronic visitors for skin, partners of PLHIV receiving private anti- retroviral therapy (ART), partners of newly diagnosed PLHIV in private labs, in addition to KPs and high-risk individuals accessing private services. In this model, the project recruited private providers mapped and working with NACO supported programs. Communication materials developed by the project were displayed at the clinics, including videos, for generating demand for HIVST, in addition to the project undertaking demand generation activities in areas with KPs around the selected clinics. The trained private provider conducted eligibility assessment, did pre-test counselling, demonstration HIVST through the use of videos and other job aids, and helped the participants choose an HIVST kit, either oral fluid-based or blood-based, and the mode of assistance (assisted or unassisted). PATH provided the HIVST kits to the private providers through the participating project partner. Based on the result of HIVST, the private provider and the participating project partner followed the algorithm for post-test counselling, confirmatory test (for those who had reactive or indeterminate results with HIVST) and on, treatment and care support. This model was implemented with private providers in five states – Gujarat, Karnataka, Telangana, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal – with SAATHII as the lead implementing partner. Model#3: Workplace model: PATH collaborated with ILO partners, namely, Brihanmumbai Electric Supply & Transport Undertaking (BEST) of the Municipal Corporation Greater Mumbai (MCGM) and the Transport Corporation of India Foundation (TCIF), to extend HIVST services to formal employees, self-identified high-risk individuals, such as truckers and informal labour workforce, partners/ clients of high-risk individuals and KPs and partners of PLHIV. In this model, staff from workplace interventions with the two organizations used the Information Education Communication/Behavioral Change Communication (IEC/BCC) materials developed by the project for community awareness and demand generation for HIVST through community events and interpersonal communication and conducted the eligibility assessment. The service providers were trained to conduct pre-test counselling, demonstration HIVST through the use of videos, and other job aids, and help the participants choose an HIVST kit and their preferred mode of assistance. They also connected the HIVST users to facilities for confirmatory test, treatment and care services, depending on the result of HIVST. Model#4: PLHIV network-led model: The PLHIV network-led model was implemented through the Network of Maharashtra People with HIV (NMP+) which is a PLHIV network under the National Coalition of People Living with HIV/AIDS (NCPI+). Through this model, HIVST was distributed through the community run pharmacy, the TAAL pharmacy, which provides subsidized ART to PLHIV and offers HIV testing and prevention services to all people at a high- risk of HIV, and through the outreach support provided to PLHIV. This model aimed to reach the partners of PLHIV and other clients who use the network’s services. Through this model, HIVST was distributed across five districts in the state of Maharashtra. Model#5: Virtual model: The virtual model followed the digital marketplace approach. The project developed the www.sahayindia.org website for potential participants to visit and order test kits from. The project ran a digital campaign and reached out to potential members of KPs, high-risk individuals, their partners as well as the partners of PLHIV through search engine optimization and social media promotion through platforms, such as Facebook, Instagram, and others. 11 Interested participants were guided to the SAHAY India website. On the landing page of the website, eligibility assessment was conducted, participants’ status was digitally validated, their consent was taken online, and a unique user identification (UID) was generated. The participants could then virtually place order for the HIVST kit of their choice and had the choice of ordering the test kit through courier or visit a nearby project site for in-person pickup. The test kit was couriered to them along with IEC materials and information for use (IFU), after an online pre-test counselling. For in-person pickups, participants would receive pre-test counselling in person and seek HIVST through assisted or unassisted mode. Both types of participants, those receiving the HIVST kits online, and those undertaking the HIVST from a project site, were followed-up for results, and post-test counselling and were encouraged to share the test results with the appropriate health service provider. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Any person more than or equal to 18 years of age, able and willing to give written informed consent, were considered eligible for the study. Illiterate participants could be enrolled in presence of a witness trusted by the participant. Additionally, participants had to identify themselves as a member of a KP group (MSM, FSW, PWID, TG/H), a partner or client of a KP, a partner of PLHIV, as an employee of a participating industry, or a referral by a collaborating private practitioner to be eligible for inclusion in the study. Participants who identified themselves at risk of HIV were also considered eligible for inclusion in the study. Additionally, participants for the virtual model had to provide a verifiable phone number to be included in the study. Furthermore, anyone who reported as a known case of HIV-positive, on ART at the time of the study, had taken pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), or was pregnant were excluded from the study. Participants who were enrolled once in the study were not eligible for re-enrolment, unless there was a compelling reason for retesting. Additionally, participants who reported that they have undergone test recently for Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, or Human T-lymphotropic Virus (HTLV) were not eligible to use the oral fluid-based OraQuick® test kit. Capacity strengthening PATH strengthened the capacities of peer educators, counsellors, and service provides engaged in this project through a cascading training model. PATH developed a detailed learning resource package (LRP) consisting of training modules, facilitators guide, implementation protocols, standard operating procedures, IEC/BCC materials, IFU, and other learning materials. This was then used during a 3-day training of trainers (TOTs) from all implementation partners. The master trainers further trained the field-level implementation staff through a series of trainings, where members of PATH, and representatives of CAB and SOCs were present to mentor and guide the training roll-out. PATH and members of the implementing partners, based on the findings and results of the online assessment, conducted refresher training or provided one-on-one mentoring support. All training participants were encouraged to respond to a set of questions on a Google form, which was analyzed to understand the thematic areas, where the learning required further reinforcement through virtual support and mentoring. Furthermore, state managers, and members of CAB, SOC, and CMB visited the project sites to give supportive supervision for implementation. 12 Communication strategy Encouraging members of KPs, self-identified high-risk individuals, partners of high-risk individuals, and PLHIV, among others, to become knowledgeable about HIVST and accept it for use was a key component for improving demand, feasibility, and acceptability of HIVST. PATH, using the findings of the formative assessment and with support of a communication agency, conceptualized, designed, field-tested and developed a communication package. The package consisted of taglines, IFU in print and videos, counselling videos, and point-of-use promotional products, among others. These products were first developed in Hindi, and then further translated into seven regional languages and made available at project sites for use. In addition to the products, the communication package included guidance for the most effective use in various intervention settings. The IEC/BCC products were shared with implementing partners and their staff during trainings, site visits, and virtual mentoring sessions, and they were oriented on its use. Independent site evaluation SHARE India, one of the implementing partners, conducted site evaluations of 10% of the project sites to monitor and report on adherence to the protocols for the study. The site monitoring was conducted using a standardized checklist and with prior information to the implementing partners. The checklist monitored adherence to SOPs at the project site and individual staff levels. Any deviations from the protocols were reported using a standardized site monitoring report on a Share India microsite within 24 hours, with PATH mandated to take actions and submit an action taken report within another 24 hours of receiving the report. Corrective actions in the form of training, and virtual and onsite mentoring were taken in case of minor deviations. However, if any site reported a score of less than 75% on the monitoring checklist, then the implementation at that site was immediately stopped. The staff members were then required to undergo intensive training. After the training an assessment was conducted, and only after the staff passed this assessment, they were allowed to restart distribution. Initiatives to disseminate of the best practices, transition , and scale-up of HIVST The capacity strengthening of various implementing partners – PEPFAR partners, Global Fund partners, ILO partners, NACO’s TI partners, besides the other implementing partners of this project has provided the foundation for rapid scaling up of HIVST in India. PATH has initiated the writing of scientific papers and publishing the findings of the project in peer reviewed scientific journals to contribute to the growing knowledge base on HIVST. Besides this, we are in the process of disseminating the findings, lessons from this project and the conclusions on the national, regional, and global platforms. However, the biggest impetus to scaling up HIVST in India is the level of interest and attention HIVST is gaining in the national policy discourse. NACO’s Technical Working Group (TWG) has published a white paper on HIVST. Moreover, the National AIDS Control Plan, Phase V (NACP 5) has indicated the roll-out of self-testing as one of its deliverables. This intent has been reiterated in the Sampoorna Suraksha Strategy (SSS) of NACP-5. Furthermore, the virtual intervention strategy under NACP-5 further underpins the national commitment to enhancing access to HIVST. 13 Challenges and its mitigation The project experienced a few challenges, right from its start. Some of the challenges were due to the novelty of HIVST testing and the lack of familiarity with the study procedures, while others were either administrative or part of the learning process. All challenges to the project were rigorously analyzed for their root causes and mitigation strategies were evolved in consultation with PISPAG and CAB and implemented. Time-consuming approval processes: HIVST was new to India. There were no approved manufacturers, no clear policy guidelines or protocols and no studies conducted earlier on HIVST in the country. When PATH initiated the project to understand the demand, feasibility, and acceptability of HIVST in the country, there was no precedence in the country to learn from. As a result, PATH learnt on the way that a project to evaluate a new scientific technique or a new technology required several different approvals (from national to global ethics committees), regulatory approval, and test licenses, among others. However, each of the approvals was essential for the study to happen. In this case, this entire process of getting all necessary approvals took over 18 months of the project time. Community engagement and ownership: Besides the technical approvals, PATH laid emphasis on community ownership and their engagement. As various communities were participating in the project, they also had different needs and understanding of the project. Ensuring that all expectations of all stakeholders are aligned with the project objectives and their considerations are incorporated in the study protocols required several rounds of active engagement and iterations. This was done by establishing committees of representatives from the communities and engaging them in all stages of project implementation. Furthermore, the project team presented the project implementation design to the Community System Streghtening Technical Working Group, which has representation of key communities and received their concurrence to implement with CBOs and key communities' representatives. All study products – protocols, tools and communication and training package were reviewed by the CAB, with the SOCs and CMBs playing an active role in overseeing the on-ground implementation. Furthermore, they were involved in reviewing and approving the consent form for participants, ensuring that the key concerns of affected communities. Study tools, communication package and consent form in multiple languages: The project had initially visualized the consent forms, study tools, communication packages, and all tools in Hindi. Acknowledging that the participants, peer educators and service providers need to be familiar and comfortable with the tools provided to them for the study, PATH got their entire study toolkit translated, and the final products were made available in eight languages, namely, Hindi, English, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali. This was a time-consuming process, which required several rounds of review and iterations before the tools were customized to local requirements and approved by NACO, the PISPAG and CAB for use in the project. Limited resources: The scope of the study expanded significantly from the original, approved proposal, as newer tasks, such as translations and a wider range of stakeholder engagement got added to the project mandate. The project had limited resources to accommodate these additions. CDC through PEPFAR stepped up and absorbed the cost of training, in addition to supporting the implementation and monitoring of HIVST activities in their cluster districts. Other partners, such as ILO, chipped in with smaller sized grants and helped the rollout of HIVST pilot in workplace settings. 14 Key results Enrolment The study staff conducted eligibility assessment for a total of 97, 238 participants. Among these, 172 participants were found ineligible to receive the HIVST kit. Among the ineligible participants, 66 were pregnant, 50 were known HIV-positive cases, 31 reported to be on ART, and 25 returned to be reincluded. Overall, 2,799 participants refused to be enrolled. In total, 94,267 participants were included in the study. The study cascade is detailed in Figure 2. Figure 2: Study cascade Among the 94,267 participants who were enrolled, 93,380 participants received the HIVST kit s. Among the 889 who enrolled but did not get the test kits, 518 were enrolled through the workplace model, 267 though the virtual model, 84 though the community -led model, 17 through the PLHIV network-led model, and three from the private practitioner model. Overall, 96.2% (93,380/97,066) of eligible participants accepted HIVST kits. 15 Model-wise enrolment The community -based model enrolled 79,324 participants ( Figure 3). The private practitioner model contributed to 7.5% (6,984) of the enrolment, followed by the workplace model (5.6%), PLHIV network-led model (1.8%) and virtual model (0.2%). Figure 3: Model-wise enrolment (N=93,380) Among the 14 states where the enrolment was carried out, most participants were enrolled from Gujarat (14.0%), followed by Karnataka (12.9%) and Tamil Nadu (12.0%) (Figure 4). Distribution started in Uttar Pradesh in June 2022 and 466 participants were enrolled. Figure 4: State-wise enrolment 16 Model-wise enrolment per state: The community-based and the virtual models were implemented in all 14 states. The private practitioner model was implemented in five states, namely, Karnataka, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and West Bengal. The PLHIV network -led model was implemented only in Maharashtra. The workplace model was implemented in Punjab, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and West Bengal. Highest recruitment for the community -based model happened in Tamil Nadu (13.8%), closely followed by Karnataka (13.3%). In the private practitioner model, most recruitment was from the states of Telangana (42.7%) and Gu jarat (40.5%). The PLHIV network-led model was implemented only in Maharashtra. The virtual model saw major contribution from Gujarat (46.5%) and Andhra Pradesh (33.2%). The workplace model saw significant enrolment from Maharashtra (35.3%) and Punjab (31.0%). District-wise enrolment : The study was implemented in 50 districts across the 14 states. The district-wise distribution is shown in Figure 5. Figure 5: District-wise test kit distribution 17 Gender-wise distribution Overall, 63,341 (67.8%) of participants who were given the test kits identified themselves as males, 25,248 (27.0%) identified as females, and 4,742 (5.1%) identified as transgender ( Figure 6). A small proportion of the participants (949, 0.1%) preferred not to disclose their gender . Most transgender people (41.6%) were enrolled from Delhi and Tamil Nadu. Model -wise, there were differences in the gender -wise enrollment (Figure 7) . Almost all participants enrolled (99.5%) through the workplace model were men , while, in the PLHIV network-led model that targeted partners of PLHIV, 51% enrolled were women. Figure 6: Gender distribution (N=93,351) Figure 7: Model-wise gender distribution 18 Population groups The highest proportion of participants included in the study identified themselves at a high risk of HIV (24.8%) (Figure 8). Almost half (48.8%) of the participants identified themselves as belonging to one of the KP groups, with FSWs being the highest. Figure 8: Population group wise enrolment (N=93,351) The population groups enrolled per model depended on the target population for each of these groups (Table 1). The community-based model reached all the four KP groups, their partners and clients, and self-identified high-risk individuals. More than half (52.2%) the participants in the PLHIV network-led model were partners or family members of PLHIV. The virtual model reached mainly to MSMs (78.5%). This proportion of those preferring HIVST was highest among participants from the PLHIV network -led model (97.5%: 1 ,627/1,668) and the wor kplace model (97.4%: 5,080/5,217). The proportion of those preferring HIVST for future testing was 88.7% (70,391/79,317) for the community-based model, 88.6% (164/185) for the virtual model, and 72.3% (5,046/6,984) for the private practitioners’ model (Table 5). Among KP groups, 86.8% participants reported that they would prefer HIVST for their future testing needs over other testing modalities, while among other high -risk groups, 89.4% participants reported that they will prefer HIVST.
