all_items.content: Home HIV-Duo Test # HIV Test (HIV-Duo Test) Also known as: HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/ P24 Ag Duo Test) 72+ booked in last 3 days No special precautions Sample Type **Blood** Report **Within 6 Hours** Recommended for **Male, Female** NABL & CAP Accredited Labs Accurate & Quality Test Reports Home Collection in 60 Minutes Trusted by Leading Doctors & Hospitals ## HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/ P24 Ag Duo Test) Details in Brief | | | | --- | --- | | Also Known As | HIV 4th Generation Test, HIV Antigen/Antibody Combination Test, HIV-1/2 Ab & P24 Ag Test | | Purpose | Detects both HIV P24 antigen and HIV antibodies, helps diagnose early and late-stage HIV infections, and supports rapid and accurate HIV screening. | | Preparation | Clinical History Required | | Fasting | Not required | | Reporting Time | After 6 hours | | Cost | 720 | ## ****What Is an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test)?**** The HIV-Duo test is an advanced 4th-generation screening test designed to detect Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection. The test helps detect both early signs of HIV infection and your body's immune response to the virus, enabling doctors to diagnose HIV sooner than older-generation tests. This comprehensive test uses a blood sample collected from a vein in your arm to provide accurate results. ## ****What Does the HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Measure?**** The HIV-Duo test simultaneously measures important markers in your blood to provide accurate HIV screening: * **P24 Antigen**: A protein that forms part of the HIV, detectable very early after infection. * **HIV-1 Antibodies**: Your body's immune response proteins against the most common type of HIV worldwide. * **HIV-2 Antibodies**: Immune response proteins against the less common HIV type found mainly in West Africa but also present in India. ## ****HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test): Who Needs It and Why It's Done**** ### ****What Symptoms May Call for an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test)?**** Your doctor may recommend this test if you experience flu-like symptoms that appear 2 to 4 weeks after potential HIV exposure: * Fever and chills * Persistent sore throat * Unexplained skin rash * Muscle aches and joint pain * Extreme tiredness or fatigue * Swollen lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, or groin * Mouth ulcers ### ****Who Should Get an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 AG Duo Test)?**** This test is recommended for various groups to ensure early detection and appropriate care: * **Individuals with symptoms**: Anyone experiencing early HIV symptoms, especially after potential exposure. * **High-risk individuals**: People with unprotected sexual contact, multiple partners, or a needle-sharing history. * **Routine screening**: Everyone aged 13-64 as part of regular healthcare check-ups. * **Pregnant women**: All expectant mothers to prevent transmission to their baby. * **After potential exposure**: Anyone who believes they may have been exposed to HIV. ### ****Why Is an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Done?**** This test enables early and accurate HIV detection. It allows prompt medical treatment, helps manage the virus effectively, and significantly reduces the transmission risk to others. ## ****Importance of an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test)**** The HIV-Duo test is clinically significant because it reduces the window period for detection. By looking for both the P24 antigen and antibodies, it can identify HIV infection as early as 2-4 weeks after exposure. Early diagnosis allows you to start antiretroviral therapy promptly, which suppresses the virus to undetectable levels. This protects your immune system, helps you live a healthy life, and prevents AIDS progression. When your viral load becomes undetectable through treatment, you cannot transmit HIV to sexual partners, making early testing a powerful tool for stopping HIV spread. ## ****HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Booking & Reports – Metropolis Healthcare India**** ### ****How to Book an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test)?**** 1. **Simple Online Booking** Booking can be done through the Metropolis Healthcare App or website. Select 'HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test)', choose a convenient time slot, and provide your address for a blood test at home. You can also visit the nearest Metropolis Lab if you prefer to give the sample directly at the lab. 2. **Safe Home Sample Collection** Our trained phlebotomists ensure the timely collection of your sample while strictly following all safety and hygiene protocols. 3. **Sample Tracking Updates** Stay informed at every step. From collection to testing, you can track your sample directly through the Metropolis Healthcare website. 4. **Accurate Laboratory Testing** Your sample is processed at our NABL- & CAP-accredited laboratories, where expert technicians ensure accurate results. 5. **Quick & Easy Reports** Receive your test reports promptly via email, WhatsApp, or by downloading them directly from the Metropolis Healthcare website or app. ### ****Is Home Sample Collection for the HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 AG Duo Test) Available Near You?**** Yes, home sample collection for the HIV-Duo Test is widely available across India through Metropolis Healthcare. Our trained phlebotomists follow strict safety protocols while collecting your blood sample in the comfort of your home. This service eliminates travel concerns and waiting times, making HIV screening more accessible. ### ****How Long Does It Take to Get an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Report?**** Reports are usually available within 6 hours once the sample reaches the lab. ### ****Where Can I See or Get HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 AG Duo Test) Results?**** Test results from Metropolis Healthcare can be accessed through multiple convenient channels. You can log in to the Metropolis website using your credentials or use the Metropolis Healthcare App to view and download your reports. Additionally, test reports are sent via email or WhatsApp, and you also have the option to collect a physical copy directly from the lab. ## ****Interpreting HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Results**** ### ****What Your HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Results May Indicate**** The following table explains how to understand your HIV-Duo test results and their clinical significance: | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Parameter** | **Reference Range** | **Non-Reactive Result** | **Reactive Result** | | HIV-DUO (IVth Generation Test) | Non-reactive: = 1.0 S/CO | No HIV antigens or antibodies detected - normal result | HIV antigens or antibodies detected — requires confirmatory testing. | ## ****Conditions that May Affect HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Accuracy**** Several factors can influence your HIV-Duo test results and should be considered when interpreting outcomes: * Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) medications may affect test accuracy. * A very early infection stage (within the window period) might yield false-negative results. * Unknown HIV variants may lead to negative findings despite infection. * Late-stage HIV infection, in rare cases, may show unusual patterns. * Autoimmune conditions or certain medications might cause false-positive reactions. * Recent vaccinations could potentially interfere with antibody detection. * Sample quality issues, such as haemolysis or inappropriate storage temperature. ## ****How Is an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Done?**** The HIV-Duo test follows a straightforward blood collection procedure performed by trained healthcare professionals: * A healthcare professional cleans the area on your arm with an antiseptic. * An elastic band is tied around your upper arm to make veins more visible. * A small needle is inserted into a vein to collect blood. * About 3 ml of blood is drawn into a special collection tube. * The needle is removed, and a bandage is applied to the site. * Your blood sample is sent to the laboratory for analysis using advanced immunoassay technology. ## ****How Should You Prepare for an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test)?**** Preparing for your HIV-Duo test is simple and requires minimal effort on your part: * **No fasting required**: You can eat and drink normally before the test. * **Continue regular medications**: Take your usual medicines unless advised otherwise by your doctor. * **Inform about HIV prevention drugs**: Tell your doctor if you're taking PrEP or PEP medications. * **Provide clinical history**: Share relevant medical information with your doctor. * **Wear comfortable clothing**: Choose clothes that allow easy access to your arms. ## ****Diseases that an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Can Help Detect**** This comprehensive test helps identify and diagnose several HIV-related conditions: * **HIV-1 infection**: The most common type of HIV found worldwide. * **HIV-2 infection**: A less common HIV variant primarily found in West Africa. * **Acute HIV infection**: Very early-stage HIV before full antibody development. * **Chronic HIV infection**: Established HIV infection with detectable antibodies. * **Asymptomatic HIV**: HIV infection without obvious symptoms or signs. ## ****HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Packages that You Can Book With Metropolis Healthcare**** Metropolis Healthcare offers comprehensive testing packages that include HIV screening along with other important health assessments: | | | | --- | --- | | **Test/Package Name** | **Purpose/Highlights** | | HIV Early Detection Profile-1 | Comprehensive early HIV screening for individuals over 2, with additional parameters to support early intervention and treatment. | | STD Profile-I Test | Basic sexually transmitted disease screening panel. | | STD Profile-II Test | Expanded screening for STIs, including additional pathogens. | ## ****HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) Prices in Different Cities**** The cost of an HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/P24 Ag Duo Test) may vary depending on your location. Here's a table showing the approximate prices in different cities: | | | | --- | --- | | **City** | **Price (INR)** | | HIV-Duo Test Price in Mumbai | ₹ 400 to ₹ 1000 | | HIV-Duo Test Price in Delhi | ₹ 400 to ₹ 1000 | | HIV-Duo Test Price in Bangalore | ₹ 400 to ₹ 1000 | | HIV-Duo Test Price in Chennai | ₹ 400 to ₹ 1000 | | HIV-Duo Test Price in Pune | ₹ 400 to ₹ 1000 | | HIV-Duo Test Price in Ahmedabad | ₹ 400 to ₹ 1000 | Read More ## HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/ P24 Ag Duo Test) Price Metropolis Healthcare is a leading diagnostics centre and pathology lab in India equipped with the latest state-of-the-art technologies that provides the HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/ P24 Ag Duo Test) with a clear pricing structure. The HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/ P24 Ag Duo Test) Price in Mumbai is ₹ 720 . We are committed to deliver accurate and quality results from the best labs in India with complete transparency regarding test cost and turnaround time. No matter where you are, we strive to offer patients high-quality service that is affordable and accessible. ## Frequently Asked Questions There are three main types: antigen/antibody combination tests (like HIV-Duo), antibody-only tests, and nucleic acid tests. The HIV-Duo test is highly recommended, as it detects both antigens and antibodies, providing earlier and more accurate results than other tests. For the HIV-Duo test, the optimal time is 18-45 days after potential exposure. This allows sufficient time for both P24 antigens and antibodies to develop to detectable levels, ensuring accurate results while minimising the window period. No, fasting is not required for HIV testing. You can eat and drink normally before the test. The presence of HIV antigens and antibodies in your blood is not affected by food intake or fasting status. Dehydration does not affect the accuracy of HIV test results for detecting antigens or antibodies. However, severe dehydration may make blood collection more difficult for the technician, so staying adequately hydrated is recommended for comfort during the procedure. No special dietary preparation is needed. Continue taking your regular medications, but inform your doctor about all medicines, especially HIV prevention drugs like PrEP or PEP, as these may potentially affect test interpretation and timing. A healthcare professional cleans your arm with an antiseptic, ties an elastic band around your upper arm, inserts a small needle into your vein, and collects blood in a special tube. The entire procedure takes less than five minutes. ### Are there any risks to the test? Risks are minimal and similar to any routine blood test. You may experience slight pain, minor bruising at the needle site, or occasional dizziness. Serious complications, like infection, are extremely rare when proper protocols are followed. ### What level of HIV test is normal? HIV test results are reported as either non-reactive (normal) with values less than 1.0 S/CO or reactive (preliminary positive) with values of 1.0 S/CO or higher. A non-reactive result means no HIV infection was detected. ### What is an HIV test also known as? The HIV-Duo test is also called the HIV 4th Generation Test, the HIV Antigen/Antibody Combination Test, or the HIV-1/2 Ab & p24 Ag Test. All these names refer to the same advanced screening method that detects both antigens and antibodies. ### Is the HIV test accurate? Yes, modern HIV tests, including the HIV-Duo, are extremely accurate, with over 99% reliability when performed correctly after the window period. All reactive screening results require confirmatory testing to establish a definitive diagnosis, ensuring maximum accuracy. ### How early can HIV be detected? The HIV-Duo test can typically detect HIV infection as early as 18 days after exposure, though it may take up to 45 days for definitive results. This makes it one of the earliest detection methods available for HIV screening. ### Ratings & Reviews (0) No reviews available ### Why Metropolis? We offer a comprehensive range of 4000+ clinical laboratory tests and profiles, which are used for prediction, early detection, diagnostic screening, confirmation and/or monitoring of the disease. 170+ Advanced Labs Trusted by Leading Doctors & Hospitals Over 2000+ Scientific Officers Proficiency Testing for Accurate Reports ## HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/ P24 Ag Duo Test) Price ₹ 720 MORE WAYS TO BOOK Book a Home Visit Now Book any blood test or health checkup and get tested at the comfort of your home Most Frequently Booked Test * Food Intolerance (Food IgG) Test, Serum ₹16,000 * CBC Haemogram, EDTA Blood ₹340 * Thrombophilia Profile-Maxi ₹18,500 * Vitamin D Test (25-Hydroxy) ₹1,800 * HbA1c- Glycated Haemoglobin, EDTA Blood ₹640 * STD Screening Advanced ₹8,800 More Related Tests * Tacrolimus Test ₹5,000 * Homocysteine Test ₹1,450 * Anti Mullerian Hormone (AMH) Test ₹2,400 * Ferritin Test ₹1,000 * Prolactin Test (PRL) ₹650 * CRP Test (C-Reactive Protein) ₹620 * CA-125 (Cancer Antigen-125) Test ₹1,550 ## Our Blog Take a look at some of the related content from our blog HIV-Duo Test (HIV1&2 Ab/ P24 Ag Duo Test) is added to cart #### Book a Home Visit Now! 080-4891-1400 WhatsApp Get a Call Back

all_items.title: HIV Screening Test: MedlinePlus Medical Test
all_items.content: ## What is an HIV test? An HIV test checks a sample of your blood, saliva (spit), or urine (pee) to see whether you are infected with HIV (human immunodeficiency virus). HIV is a virus that destroys certain cells in your immune system. These cells protect your body against diseases from germs, such as bacteria, viruses, and fungi. If you lose too many immune cells, your body will have trouble fighting off infections and other diseases. HIV is spread through contact with blood and other body fluids from a person who has an HIV infection. This usually happens during sex or when sharing needles or other items used to inject drugs. HIV is the virus that causes AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome). AIDS is the final, most serious stage of an HIV infection. Without treatment, HIV gradually destroys your immune system, which leads to AIDS. With AIDS, your body has trouble fighting off infections from germs that usually don't cause problems in healthy people. These are called opportunistic infections, and they can become life-threatening. AIDS increases your risk of developing certain cancers, too. Most people with HIV don't have AIDS. If you have HIV and you take HIV medicines as prescribed, you may never get AIDS. Getting tested for HIV helps catch the virus early so you can start treatment, stay healthy, and avoid spreading HIV. If you think you were exposed to HIV, talk with your health care provider right away about emergency treatment, called PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis). PEP may prevent an HIV infection if it is started within three days after a possible exposure. The sooner you start, the better. You will need to have HIV tests during and after taking PEP. There are three main types of HIV tests. They are all very accurate, but no test can find HIV in your body immediately after you're infected. That's because it can take weeks until the signs of HIV in your body increase enough to show up on a test. The time between infection and when a test can find HIV depends on your body's response to HIV and the type of test you have: * HIV antibody tests look for HIV antibodies in your blood, saliva, or urine. HIV antibodies are disease-fighting proteins that your immune system makes when you have an HIV infection. Some people make antibodies faster than others. An antibody test may find HIV antibodies as early as 23 days after infection, but it may take as long as 90 days before your body makes enough antibodies to show up on this test. Antibody tests can be done in different ways: + Lab tests use a blood sample taken from a vein. In general, lab tests can find antibodies sooner after infection than other HIV antibody tests. Test results are usually ready a few days after your blood sample is taken. + Rapid tests use saliva, urine, or blood from your finger. They provide results in about 30 minutes. + At-home tests include rapid self-test kits with everything you need to collect and test a sample of saliva on your own and get your results. With mail-in tests, you collect a drop of blood from your finger to send to a lab for testing. * HIV antibody/antigen tests are the most commonly used HIV tests. They look for HIV antibodies and antigens in your blood. An antigen is the part of the HIV virus that triggers your immune system to fight the infection. After an HIV exposure, antigens will show up in your blood sooner than antibodies: + Lab tests that use a blood sample from a vein can find an HIV infection as soon as 18 to 45 days after you were infected. + Rapid tests use a drop of blood from your finger. This test can find HIV infections starting between 18 days to 90 days after you were infected. + At-home tests, or mail-in tests, allow you to collect blood from your finger at home to send to a lab for testing. Like rapid tests, these tests can start finding HIV 18 to 90 days after infection. * NAT tests (nucleic acid tests) look for HIV in a sample of your blood taken from a vein and tested in a lab. These tests may also be called "viral load tests." They can usually find an HIV infection as soon as 10 to 33 days after infection. But they are mostly used for monitoring HIV treatment and not for routine screening, because they are expensive. Ask your provider about having a NAT test as soon as possible if you: + May have been exposed to HIV and have symptoms, such as: - Flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, aches - Extreme fatigue - Swollen lymph nodes (in your neck, groin, or armpit) - Rash - Sores in your mouth - Night sweats - Sore throat - Unexplained weight loss + Know you were exposed to HIV * May have been exposed to HIV and have symptoms, such as: Other names: HIV antibody/antigen tests, HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibody and antigen evaluation, HIV test, human immunodeficiency virus antibody test, type 1, HIV p24 antigen test ## What is it used for? An HIV screening test is used to find out if you have been infected with HIV. It may be done as a routine test or after a possible exposure to find out if you were infected with HIV. If HIV is found early, you can take medicines to protect your health so you don't get AIDS. Medicines can also help you avoid spreading HIV to others. ## Why do I need an HIV test? The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that everyone between the ages of 13 and 64 get tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care. You may need to be tested more than once if you have a higher risk for infection. If your last HIV test was more than a year ago, you should get tested as soon as possible if you have: * Had vaginal or anal sex with someone who has HIV (HIV positive) or whose HIV status you don't know * Injected drugs and shared needles, syringes, or other drug items with other people * Exchanged sex for money or drugs * Had a sexually transmitted infection (STI), such as syphilis * Had sex with anyone who has done anything listed above If you regularly do any of the things on the above list, you should be tested for HIV at least once every year. Certain people, including men who have sex with men (MSM), may benefit from being tested more often, depending on their risk. Ask your provider how often you should be tested. If you have had hepatitis or tuberculosis, you should also get tested for HIV at least once a year. If you are pregnant, your doctor may order an HIV test. That's because HIV can be passed to the fetus during pregnancy and to the baby at birth, and through breast milk. There are medicines you can take during pregnancy and delivery that greatly reduce your risk of spreading HIV to your baby. ## What happens during an HIV test? There are many places to get tested for HIV, including at your health care provider's office, health clinics, testing programs in your community, and at home. If you go somewhere for your test, a staff person or counselor will explain what type of sample will be taken and how. If you do a test at home, be sure to follow all the instructions that come with your test kit. * For blood from a vein, a health care professional will take a blood sample from a vein in your arm, using a small needle. After the needle is inserted, a small amount of blood will be collected into a test tube or vial. You may feel a little sting when the needle goes in or out. This usually takes less than five minutes. * For blood from a finger, a health care professional will use a special tool (lancet) to prick your finger and collect a sample of blood. If you are collecting your own blood sample to send to a lab, follow the instructions that come with your collection kit. * For a saliva sample, a health care professional will wipe a special swab along your gums. If you are doing an at-home test, you will do this yourself by following the instructions that come with your collection kit. * For a urine sample, a health care professional may give you a cleansing wipe, a small container, and instructions for how to collect your urine sample. Once you've collected your sample, your provider will tell you what to do next with it. ## Will I need to do anything to prepare for the test? You don't need any special preparations for an HIV test. If you are getting tested in a health clinic or community program, a counselor may talk with you about your risk for HIV. So, you may want to write down any questions you have ahead of time. ## Are there any risks to the test? There is very little risk to having any HIV screening test. If you have blood taken from a vein, you may have slight pain or bruising at the spot where the needle was put in, but most symptoms go away quickly. ## What do the results mean? A negative test result means that no signs of an HIV infection were found in your sample. But that doesn't always mean that you don't have HIV. You could have an HIV infection, but it's too soon for the test to tell and you may need another test later. Your provider or an HIV counselor can explain your test result and let you know if you need another test. In general, if you have a negative result on a rapid test or an at-home test and a possible HIV exposure that was: * 90 days ago or longer, you can be confident that you don't have HIV * Less than 90 days ago, you will likely need another test later to check for HIV again A positive test result means that signs of an HIV infection were found in your sample. You will need a follow-up test to confirm an HIV diagnosis unless you had a NAT test. * If you used an at-home test, see your provider for follow-up testing. * If you had your test at a medical office or community program, the testing site will arrange your follow-up test. If your follow-up test is also positive, it means you have HIV. It's important to start medicines called antiretroviral therapy (ART) right away, even if you're still healthy. ART can't cure HIV, but it may lower the amount of virus in your blood enough so that a test can't find it. If you're living with HIV, it's important to see your provider regularly for tests to check how your treatment is working. about laboratory tests, reference ranges, and understanding results. ## Is there anything else I need to know about HIV screening? HIV testing can be anonymous. That means you do not have to give your name when you take an HIV test. Instead, you'll receive a number. To get your test results, you'll give the number instead of your name. ## References 1. AIDSinfo [Internet]. all_items.title: HIV Test Types, Procedure, Timing & Results Explained
all_items.content: #### Preventive Healthcare # HIV Test: Types, Procedure, Timing and Results Last Updated On: Jul 28 2026 Share --- ## **What is an HIV Test?** An HIV test is a diagnostic test that detects the presence of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in blood or oral fluid by identifying antibodies, antigens (p24 protein), or viral genetic material (RNA). When HIV enters the body, it triggers an immune response that produces antibodies—proteins made by the immune system to fight infection. Simultaneously, the virus produces antigens such as the p24 protein, which appear in the blood within 2–4 weeks after infection. Modern HIV test procedures can detect these antibodies, antigens, or even the virus's genetic material directly. ## **Why HIV Testing is Important** Early detection through HIV testing allows you to begin treatment promptly, which can help maintain your immune system's strength and prevent progression to AIDS. The benefits of HIV testing extend beyond personal health: * **Early treatment access:** Prompt diagnosis enables you to start antiretroviral therapy, which can reduce viral load to undetectable levels. * **Prevention of transmission:** Knowing your status helps you protect sexual partners and maintain safer practices. * **Informed health decisions:** HIV test results empower you to make educated choices about relationships and family planning. * **Peace of mind:** Regular testing provides reassurance and reduces anxiety about your HIV status. * **Public health protection:** Widespread testing helps control HIV spread in communities. ## **Types of HIV Tests** Understanding the different types of HIV tests helps you choose the most appropriate option for your situation. Each HIV test type has specific advantages, timing considerations, and accuracy levels. ### **1. Antibody HIV Test (3rd Generation ELISA or Rapid Test)** The antibody HIV test, often called an ELISA test, detects antibodies your immune system produces in response to HIV infection. This traditional HIV test procedure has been the backbone of HIV screening for decades, though it requires more time to detect recent infections compared to newer methods. Your body typically takes several weeks to produce detectable levels of HIV antibodies, which explains why the antibody HIV test has a longer window period. However, these tests remain highly reliable for detecting established infections and are widely available in healthcare settings. ### **2. Antigen/Antibody HIV Test (4th Generation)** The fourth-generation antigen/antibody HIV test represents a significant advancement in HIV testing technology. This comprehensive HIV test procedure detects both HIV antibodies and the p24 antigen, allowing for earlier detection than antibody-only tests. Fourth-generation tests can typically detect HIV infection 18–45 days after exposure, making them the preferred choice for routine screening in most healthcare settings. The combination approach significantly improves HIV test accuracy, particularly for recent infections that might be missed by antibody-only tests. ### **3. NAT (Nucleic Acid Test)** The nucleic acid test (NAT) directly detects HIV RNA in blood and is sometimes referred to as a viral load test when used for monitoring., directly detects HIV genetic material in your blood. This sophisticated HIV test procedure offers the shortest window period, typically identifying infections 10-14 days after exposure. NAT testing is particularly valuable when very recent exposure is suspected or when confirmatory testing is required after an indeterminate result. It measures the amount of HIV RNA in your blood, providing both diagnostic information and treatment monitoring capabilities for people already diagnosed with HIV. However, viral load tests are more expensive and complex than other options, so they're typically reserved for specific clinical situations. ## **How an HIV Test Works** Most HIV tests begin with sample collection, which might involve drawing blood from a vein, pricking your finger for a small blood sample, or collecting saliva using a special swab. The sample is then processed using laboratory techniques designed to identify specific markers of HIV infection. Laboratory analysis typically involves exposing your sample to reagents that react with HIV components. For antibody tests like the ELISA test, the process identifies immune proteins that bind specifically to HIV. Antigen tests look for viral proteins, while nucleic acid tests amplify and detect HIV genetic material using sophisticated molecular techniques. ## **HIV Test Window Period** The window period—the time between HIV infection and when tests can reliably detect it—varies significantly among different HIV test types. * **Antibody tests:** 23–90 days after exposure for reliable detection (average 30 days) * **Fourth-generation antigen/antibody tests:** 18–45 days after exposure * **Nucleic acid tests (NAT):** 10–33 days after exposure, with earliest detection possible at 10–14 days * **Rapid point-of-care tests:** Detectable after approximately 30–90 days; may miss very recent infections * **Home HIV tests:** Similar to laboratory tests, but may have slightly longer window periods. ## **HIV Test Accuracy & Sensitivity** Modern HIV tests are highly reliable when done at the right time. Fourth-generation antigen/antibody tests are over 99% accurate when performed six weeks after exposure, while nucleic acid tests can detect infection even earlier with similar precision. Accuracy depends on the test type, timing, and laboratory standards. False positives are uncommon (<1%) and are always resolved with confirmatory testing, typically using a second different assay or NAT. False negatives usually occur when testing too early in the window period, making proper timing and retesting—if risk continues—important for accurate results. ## **Who Should Get an HIV Test?** * Individuals with multiple or new sexual partners * People who share injection equipment or needles * Pregnant women as part of routine prenatal care * Anyone diagnosed with sexually transmitted infections * People who have had unprotected sex in high-prevalence areas * Men who have sex with men * Individuals seeking peace of mind about their HIV status * Healthcare workers following potential occupational exposure, such as needlestick injuries ## **HIV Test Procedure** The standard HIV test procedure follows established protocols designed to ensure accuracy, confidentiality, and appropriate patient care. 1. **Pre-test counselling and informed consent:** Your healthcare provider discusses the test, its implications, and obtains your permission. 2. **Sample collection:** Blood draw, finger prick, or oral swab, depending on the chosen test type. 3. **Laboratory processing:** Samples are analysed using appropriate testing methods. 4. **Quality assurance:** Results undergo verification procedures to ensure accuracy. 5. **Result communication:** Healthcare providers share findings and provide post-test counselling as needed. 6. **Follow-up planning:** Discussion of next steps based on your HIV test results. ## **HIV Test Preparation** * **No fasting required:** You can eat and drink normally before your HIV test. * **Medication disclosure:** Inform your healthcare provider about any medications you're taking. * **Recent exposure information:** Be prepared to discuss potential HIV exposures and timing. * **Emotional preparation:** Consider how you might respond to different HIV test results. * **Privacy considerations:** HIV testing is confidential and, in most countries, protected by law; anonymous testing may also be available. * **Insurance and payment:** Clarify coverage and costs beforehand. ## **How to Interpret HIV Test Results?** HIV test results typically fall into three categories: negative, positive, or indeterminate. * A negative result means no evidence of HIV infection was detected in your sample, though timing relative to potential exposure affects result reliability. * A reactive or positive screening test result indicates possible HIV infection and must be confirmed with a second, different test or NAT before diagnosis. * Indeterminate results occur rarely and typically require repeat testing. ## **What to Do if Your HIV Test is Positive?** Receiving positive HIV test results can feel overwhelming, but modern HIV treatment allows people to live long, healthy lives. Taking immediate, appropriate steps ensures you receive proper care and support. * **Seek immediate medical care**: Connect with an HIV specialist or infectious disease physician for a comprehensive evaluation. * **Confirm results**: Ensure confirmatory testing validates initial positive screening results. * **Begin treatment evaluation**: Discuss antiretroviral therapy options and treatment readiness with your healthcare team. * **Notify partners**: Inform recent sexual partners about potential exposure so they can seek testing. * **Access support services**: Connect with counselling services, support groups, and community resources. * **Lifestyle modifications**: Discuss healthy lifestyle changes that support immune function and overall well-being. * **Follow-up scheduling**: Establish regular monitoring appointments for viral load tests and CD4 counts. ## **Factors That Affect HIV Test Accuracy** * **Testing timing**: Window period considerations affect detection capabilities, particularly for recent exposures. * **Test methodology**: Different HIV test types offer varying sensitivity and specificity levels. * **Sample quality**: Proper collection and handling ensure accurate laboratory analysis. * **Laboratory standards**: Accredited facilities with quality control measures provide more reliable results. * **Medication effects**: Certain medications may theoretically affect test performance, though this is extremely rare. * **Medical conditions**: Some autoimmune conditions might cause false-positive results in rare cases. * **Technical factors**: Laboratory procedures and equipment calibration affect result accuracy. ## **At-Home HIV Test** According to the WHO, HIV self-testing with blood or oral-fluid kits is recommended as a complementary option to facility-based testing, as long as users receive clear instructions and have access to confirmatory testing and follow-up care. At-home HIV tests offer privacy and convenience, typically using oral fluid samples to deliver results in 20 – 40 minutes. about the HIV Test for guidance on how to safely and accurately conduct these tests. They reduce the need for appointments and ease the anxiety of clinical settings, but they may have longer window periods and slightly lower sensitivity for very recent infections. Any positive result should always be confirmed with a laboratory test. ## **Risks & Limitations of HIV Testing** HIV testing carries minimal physical risks, typically limited to slight discomfort from blood draws or finger pricks. However, understanding the limitations helps set appropriate expectations and ensures optimal use of testing resources. The primary limitation of HIV testing remains the window period, during which recent infections might not be detectable. Additionally, while rare, false positive and false negative results can occur, emphasising the importance of confirmatory testing and clinical correlation. Emotional responses to testing and concerns about privacy or discrimination represent additional considerations that healthcare providers address through counselling and support services. ## **When to Retest for HIV** Determining appropriate retesting intervals depends on your individual risk factors, exposure history, and previous HIV test results. Regular screening with a Viral Marker Test can help detect infections such as HIV at the appropriate time and support early diagnosis and treatment. * After potential HIV exposure, especially if initial testing occurred during the window period * Following completion of post-exposure prophylaxis treatment * When starting or discontinuing pre-exposure prophylaxis medication * During pregnancy, particularly if risk factors are present * If HIV symptoms develop, regardless of previous negative test results * As part of routine healthcare for sexually active individuals ## **Conclusion** The HIV test procedure has evolved significantly over the years. Early tests required weeks to provide results, but today's advanced testing methods can deliver accurate findings within minutes or days. This improvement has revolutionised HIV detection, enabling earlier diagnosis and treatment that can dramatically improve health outcomes. At Metropolis Healthcare, we understand the importance of accurate, confidential HIV testing. Our comprehensive portfolio of more than 4,000 tests includes all major HIV test types, from basic antibody screening to advanced viral load testing. Through our extensive network of 10,000+ touchpoints across India, we bring reliable STD testing directly to your home with professional sample collection services. ## **FAQs** ### **How soon can HIV be detected after exposure?** Nucleic acid tests can identify infections as early as 10-14 days after exposure, while fourth-generation antigen/antibody tests typically detect HIV 2-6 weeks post-exposure. Traditional antibody tests, including most ELISA tests, may require 3-12 weeks for reliable detection. ### **Can HIV be detected in a normal blood test?** No. HIV requires specific HIV tests (antigen/antibody or RNA tests). Routine blood tests cannot detect the virus. ### **Do I need to fast before an HIV test?** No. Fasting is not required before any type of HIV test. ### **Are home HIV tests accurate?** Home HIV tests are generally accurate when used according to instructions and outside the window period. However, they may have slightly longer window periods compared to laboratory-based tests and are more likely to produce false negative results for very recent infections. ### **What is the most accurate HIV test?** Fourth-generation antigen/antibody tests and nucleic acid tests represent the most accurate HIV testing options currently available. ### **Can stress or fever affect HIV test results?** No. Stress, fever, or common illnesses do not impact HIV test accuracy. ### **Is HIV curable if detected early?** No. While there is no cure for HIV, early diagnosis and consistent antiretroviral therapy (ART) allow people to live long, healthy lives with an undetectable viral load. ### **How often should I get tested for HIV?** At least once a year for all sexually active adults, and every 3–6 months for those with higher risk factors such as multiple partners or PrEP use. #### Talk to our health advisor Book Now #### Get Instant Call Back #### Most Viewed #### Featured News

Geneva: World Health Organization; 2009. ## Guidelines for Using HIV Testing Technologies in Surveillance: Selection, Evaluation and Implementation: 2009 Update. Show details ### summary #### Current HIV testing technologies and strategies * HIV testing technologies for surveillance + Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) + Rapid tests * HIV testing strategies for surveillance ## 4.1. HIV testing technologies for surveillance purposes ### 4.1.1. Overview of HIV testing For surveillance as well as diagnostic purposes in low- and middle-income countries, technologies that identify HIV antigen are expensive and technically more difficult. In most industrialized countries, current diagnostic testing procedures use an EIA to screen a specimen and, if it is reactive, the result is confirmed by testing the specimen with a western blot test. However, studies have shown that the testing algorithms using EIAs and rapid tests are as reliable for confirmation as western blots. In addition, compared with western blots, EIAs and rapid tests are less expensive, do not require as high a level of technical expertise to perform and interpret, and produce fewer indeterminate results.27, 28 Therefore, UNAIDS and WHO recommend alternative testing strategies using combinations of EIAs or rapid tests to confirm initial reactive test results.29 The tests should be highly sensitive and specific to provide reliable detection of antibodies in a specimen.30 EIAs and rapid tests contain antigens to both HIV-1 and HIV-2, and can therefore detect antibodies to both HIV types. Some tests are capable of discriminating between HIV-1 and HIV-2. EIAs and rapid tests are recommended for both HIV surveillance and diagnostic purposes because they are the most accurate and cost-effective. ### recommendation Of the available testing technologies, EIAs and rapid tests are the most practical and cost-effective for both surveillance and diagnostic purposes, and provide results comparable to an EIA/western blot algorithm. ### 4.1.2. Enzyme immunoassays #### 4.1.2.1. description EIAs rely on a primary antigen–antibody interaction and can use whole viral lysate of HIV or one or more antigens from the virus. Early EIAs produced more false-positive HIV antibody results than the current third- and fourth-generation of EIAs.27 Therefore, specimens initially found reactive when screened with an EIA were further tested with a western blot for confirmation. However, second- and third-generation EIAs have shown marked improvement in specificity as well as sensitivity, making them candidates for confirmatory tests. The use of recombinant proteins and synthetic peptides also improved the sensitivity of EIAs. The development of fourth-generation EIAs further improved detection of HIV infection due to their ability to detect both antibody towards HIV and HIVp24 antigen, which reduced the non-reactive (window) period after initial infection with HIV.30 Most HIV EIAs contain antigens to HIV-1 and HIV-2, and have been optimized to detect antibodies to both.27, 30 EIAs that detect antibodies to both HIV-1 and HIV-2 are better suited for surveillance. #### 4.1.2.2. Characteristics of EIAs EIAs are best performed at a regional or national laboratory since they require well-trained and skilled laboratory technicians, technologically advanced equipment (incubators, washers and spectrophotometers) that needs maintenance, and a constant source of electricity. EIAs are most efficient for laboratories that process a large number of specimens (90 or more) daily or for batch testing, which is common in HIV sentinel surveillance activities. Because of test design, they are not cost-effective or suitable for use on a small number of specimens. However, if a laboratory processes at least 40 specimens a day on a regular basis, EIAs may still be more appropriate than rapid tests. Because laboratories often batch specimens and run them at one time, the time before results are available may be from days to 2 or 3 weeks after collection. While this delay might be of concern for diagnostic purposes, it is not a disadvantage for unlinked anonymous testing since results are not provided back to the person, and same-day testing could lead to identification of the person tested. Since EIAs are usually performed at the regional or national level, QA and quality control (QC) measures need to be implemented in only a few laboratories (see Section 6.0). EIAs may have limited application in rural settings where the laboratory infrastructure and equipment may be insufficient (Table A) With the UN bulk procurement scheme, the cost of an EIA ranges from US$ 0.35–1.2 per test. When considering both direct and indirect costs (technology, human resources and equipment requirements), the actual cost may exceed US$ 15–20 per test.31 However, if the direct and indirect costs are shared across all programmes (blood screening, diagnosis and surveillance), a more realistic cost for surveillance activities would be US$ 4–6. #### 4.1.2.3. Performing an EIA EIAs can be performed with serum, plasma, oral fluid or DBS specimens (once eluted). They normally take between 30 minutes to up to 2 hours to perform. The manufacturer’s instructions provided with the specific EIA kit should be followed. The following are critical to the success of conducting an EIA: * Use of test kits that have not expired * Calibrated and well-maintained equipment * Adherence to dilutions and incubation times described in the manufacturer’s instructions * Use of a spectrophotometer to read results accurately and objectively * Adequate training of the technologists * Consistent source of power without outages as this would affect the storage of reagents and functioning of equipment * Use of appropriate positive and negative controls as internal quality control (IQC) reagents and use of external quality control (EQC) reagents. ### recommendation EIAs are efficient for laboratories that process large numbers of specimens daily, as is common when conducting HIV sentinel surveillance. ### 4.1.3. Rapid tests #### 4.1.3.1. description Interest in HIV antibody tests that provide same-day results and do not require additional reagents or equipment led to the availability of HIV rapid tests. Current rapid tests are based on four immunological principles: particle agglutination, immunodot (EIA), immunofiltration (flow-through device) and immunochromatography (lateral flow).2 Most HIV rapid tests contain antigens to HIV-1 and HIV-2, and detect antibodies to both strains of the virus.27, 30 A reactive test result is indicated by clumping, a spot, dot or line, depending on the test format. The sensitivity and specificity of the latest generation of rapid tests are similar to those of EIAs. Many rapid tests are under evaluation or are currently in use in low- and middle-income countries for screening, diagnostic and surveillance purposes. #### 4.1.3.2. Characteristics of rapid tests Rapid tests are useful for small laboratories that routinely perform less than 40 HIV tests per day, for laboratories without electricity or equipment, and for geographical areas with limited laboratory infrastructure. In some instances, even if a laboratory performs more than 40 tests per day but only during a limited period in a year, rapid tests may be more appropriate than EIAs. A well-organized testing facility may be able to perform up to 100 rapid tests per day (7.5 working hours) for surveillance purposes (e.g. by performing rapid tests in batches of 5–10 specimens). A result can usually be obtained in less than 30 minutes, and it is relatively easy to interpret. However, adequate training is required to correctly perform the test and interpret the results. HIV rapid test kits generally contain all the reagents needed to run the test: no additional reagents or equipment are required. Most rapid tests do not require electricity, special equipment, refrigeration or highly skilled staff, although a few that contain heat-sensitive reagents require refrigeration. Rapid tests may be appropriate for linked confidential testing among hard-to-reach populations (e.g. injecting drug users IDUS, female sex workers, MSM) or geographically remote populations. In these populations, opportunities for provision of results may be limited after the initial encounter; therefore, testing (screening and confirmatory) may need to be performed on site on the same day as specimen collection. If HIV test results are to be returned to the person tested, a confirmatory test is required (e.g. another rapid test or EIA). Rapid tests generally cost about US$ 1–3, a slightly higher cost per test than an EIA. However, rapid tests may be more cost-effective than EIAs if the additional costs of conducting an EIA are considered (e.g. equipment, laboratory infrastructure, technician training). Since there are very few steps in performing a rapid test, there is less chance for error than with an EIA. The most common error with rapid tests is not following the instructions for use as issued by the manufacturer, especially with respect to the time spent reading the results. In addition, most rapid tests include an IQC. However, when using rapid tests, QA and EQC measures need to be developed and implemented at all sites that are using them (Table A). #### 4.1.3.3. Performing a rapid test Rapid tests can be performed with serum, plasma, venous or finger-stick whole blood and oral fluid. For some rapid tests, specimen preparation may take as long as 10–20 minutes, while the simplest rapid tests require no specimen preparation. The manufacturer’s instructions provided with the test kit should be followed. Most results are easy to read and are indicated by clumping, a spot, dot or line, depending on the test format. The following are critical to the success of conducting a rapid test: * Use of test kits that have not expired * Training in the technology being used * Adherence to manufacturer’s instructions * Correct interpretation of results by person reading them ### recommendation Rapid tests are useful in settings where EIAs are not feasible or practical and in geographical areas with limited laboratory infrastructure. Rapid tests may be appropriate for hard-to-reach populations (e.g. IDUS, female sex workers, MSM) or geographically remote populations for whom HIV test results may need to be provided on site on the same day as specimen collection. ## 4.2. HIV testing strategies for surveillance ### 4.2.1. Strategy for unlinked anonymous surveillance For unlinked anonymous surveillance, the revised guidelines from WHO recommend a two-test strategy, used in a serial algorithm.32 Specimens that are reactive by both tests are considered HIV-positive for surveillance purposes. If tests are properly selected and performed, discordant results are rare. Since unlinked anonymous surveillance data are not used for individual diagnosis, no additional testing is recommended to confirm HIV seropositivity in low-prevalence epidemic states or for discordant specimens, if any. Discordant specimens (Test 1 reactive/Test 2 non-reactive) are considered as non-reactive. The selection of testing technologies and the order in which they are used (testing algorithm) are important for obtaining accurate test results. The tests should contain different antigens. They should be highly sensitive (≥99%) and highly specific (≥99%). The first test is the screening test, so it is ideal to have a more sensitive test to detect all positive results. Because some false-positives do occur, the second test needs to be highly specific to ensure that all truly negative test results are identified as negative. In addition, tests that can use serum and plasma are recommended so that multiple tests can be performed from a single specimen, avoiding the need for collection of additional specimens. For rapid tests that use oral fluid or whole blood from a finger-stick, the specimen is collected with a collection device and placed directly on the rapid test apparatus; thus, a second specimen must be collected for confirmation if the first test is reactive. Therefore, in such situations, two rapid tests should be performed simultaneously and then analysed as if performed sequentially. ### 4.2.2. Strategy for linked surveillance When surveillance makes use of linked testing or unlinked anonymous testing with informed consent (see Box 2) (e.g. among hard-to-reach populations and in national population-based surveys where participants’ HIV test results are linked to many characteristics), it is recommended to use the HIV testing strategy for diagnosis. In many surveys, either within most-at-risk populations or the general population, the strategy selected for HIV testing is linked. The participants are required to provide informed consent and the HIV test results are provided to them. Therefore, in such cases, confirmatory testing is needed according to the national guidelines or HIV testing algorithms used for HIV diagnosis. In these situations, a three-test strategy should be used regardless of the HIV prevalence level. Figure 5 presents the scheme for HIV testing in linked surveillance. If rapid tests are used for same-day return of results, there is only one opportunity during which to obtain informed consent, collect the specimens and conduct the required tests. As above, all necessary blood samples should be collected at the same time. If blood is the specimen, DBS can be prepared for QA purposes.33 ### recommendation HIV tests that can use different types of specimens (serum, plasma or DBS) are recommended so that multiple testing can be performed on the same type of specimen, avoiding the need for collection of additional specimens. * Current HIV Testing Technologies and Strategies Used in Surveillance - Guideline...Current HIV Testing Technologies and Strategies Used in Surveillance - Guidelines for Using HIV Testing Technologies in Surveillance Your browsing activity is empty. all_items.title: Guidelines and Recommendations
all_items.content: ## At a glance Many HIV professional associations and government organizations, including CDC, have developed guidelines and recommendations for HIV screening, prevention, and treatment and care. ## HIV testing Guidelines for HIV testing continue to evolve with changes in testing technology and methods to reach persons who can benefit from these services. The listed documents provide the most updated CDC guidelines on HIV testing for testing providers, program managers, and laboratory personnel. ### Guidelines HIV Infection: Detection, Counseling and Referral chapter within the STI Treatment Guidelines (2021) Provides HIV screening recommendations for persons who seek evaluation and treatment for STDs. Status: Current This MMWR policy note provides an update on CDC's initiative to assess the benefits and harms associated with more frequent screening of MSM. Laboratory Testing for the Diagnosis of HIV Infection: Updated Recommendations (2014) * Technical Update for HIV Nucleic Acid Tests Approved for Diagnostic Purposes (2023) * Technical Update Laboratory Algorithm for HIV Diagnosis (2017) * Technical Update on HIV-1/2 Differentiation Assays (2016) Provides updated recommendations for HIV testing by laboratories in the United States and describes approaches for reporting test results to persons ordering HIV tests and to public health authorities. The 2017 technical update provides information on the use of the Alere Determine HIV 1/2 Ag/Ab Combo single use rapid test (Determine) in laboratories where it is not feasible to conduct an instrumented antigen/antibody test as the initial test in the algorithm. Supporting documents: * Quick Reference Guide—Laboratory Testing for the Diagnosis of HIV Infection: Updated Recommendations (2018): A two-page summary of the recommendations. * Suggested Reporting Language for the HIV Laboratory Diagnostic Testing Algorithm (2017) Provides recommendations on testing of living and deceased donors. Provides recommendations on routine, opt-out HIV screening of adults, adolescents, and pregnant women in health care settings in the United States. Supporting documents: Status: Some sections may be out of date Provides recommendations on testing in nonclinical settings. Note: Information on HIV testing may not be consistent with latest technologies. Status: Some sections may be out of date ### Implementation Resources The following documents and webpages contain information, tools, resources and practice examples developed or funded by CDC to support implementation of guidelines. #### Nonclinical settings Grantee guidance to support the implementation of HIV testing services in nonclinical settings in the United States. The purpose of the guide is to familiarize providers with key programmatic issues and updates that impact HIV testing service delivery in nonclinical settings. Status: Current A CDC webpage that provides information and resources for providers and public on HIV testing. Status: Current Serves as a companion resource to the Planning and Implementing HIV Testing and Linkage Programs in Non-Clinical Settings: A Guide for Program Managers. Provides information, exercises, and tools to design and implement a monitoring and evaluation (M&E) strategy for HIV testing and linkage programs in non-clinical settings. Note: Information on HIV testing may not be consistent with latest technologies. Status: Some sections may be out of date #### Clinical settings A CDC webpage that provides information and resources for providers and public on HIV testing in clinical settings. Status: Current Jointly developed by CDC and The National Association of Community Health Centers, Inc. (NACHC), the document provides model, tools, and resources that health centers or primary care entity can use to rapidly launch routine HIV screening during the planning and implementation stages. Note: Information on HIV testing may not be consistent with latest technologies. Status: Some sections may be out of date ## HIV prevention The guidelines and related implementation resources below provide guidance about prevention strategies and services that can prevent or diagnose new HIV infections and link individuals at risk to relevant prevention, medical and social services. ### PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) guidelines This report presents the CDC's assessment of evidence from two randomized controlled trials of the efficacy and safety of injectable LEN, administered every 6 months subcutaneously, for HIV PrEP, and provides a clinical recommendation for its use. The recommendation in this policy note updates the 2021 CDC PrEP Clinical Practice Guideline by including LEN as an option for PrEP. Status: Current This updates the review of scientific evidence on the safety and efficacy of antiretroviral HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The update includes guidance for recommended initial and follow-up STD screening, revised HIV testing strategies, and recommended primary care practices for patients being prescribed oral or injectable PrEP. Status: Current This update provides revised checklists, patient information sheets, and billing codes for both oral and injectable PrEP and includes guidance for counseling patients about adherent PrEP use. Status: Current ### Non-occupational PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) guidelines The recommendations in these guidelines update the 2016 nPEP guidelines (CDC. Updated guidelines for antiretroviral postexposure prophylaxis after sexual, injection drug use, or other nonoccupational exposure to HIV — United States, 2016. Atlanta, GA: US Department of Health and Human Services, CDC; 2017). These 2025 nPEP guidelines update recommendations and considerations for use of HIV nPEP in the United States to include newer antiretroviral (ARV) agents, updated nPEP indication considerations, and emerging nPEP implementation strategies. The guidelines also include considerations for testing and nPEP regimens for persons exposed who have received long-acting injectable ARVs in the past. Lastly, testing recommendations for persons who experienced sexual assault were updated to align with the most recent CDC sexually transmitted infection treatment guidelines. Outlines and adapts existing general recommendations on the use of immunization and postexposure prophylaxis for tetanus and for occupational and nonoccupational exposures to bloodborne pathogens to the specific situation of a mass-casualty event. Note: Information about the use of PEP with HIV has been updated in newer guidelines. Status: Some sections may be out of date ### Occupational PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) guidelines These guidelines update the 2013 Updated US Public Health Service (PHS) Guidelines for the Management of Occupational Exposures to Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Recommendations for Postexposure Prophylaxis. The availability of new medication options, new information on the window of detection for different human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) tests, and the risk of transmission from people with undetectable viral loads prompted this update. The primary intended audience for these recommendations remains anyone involved in the provision of HIV post-exposure management to healthcare personnel (HCP). Status: Current ### Partner services Implementation Resources: This report provides updated, integrated recommendations for services provided to partners of persons with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and three other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) (i.e., syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydial infection.) Note: Some recommendations and supporting evidence have been updated in the Recommendations for HIV Prevention with Adults and Adolescents with HIV. Status: Some sections may be out of date Intended to serve as a quick reference resource and as such, lists only the recommendations and data security guidelines included in the MMWR. Note: Some of the recommendations on partner services have been updated in the Recommendations for HIV Prevention with Adults and Adolescents with HIV. Status: Some sections may be out of date ### Contraceptive use and preconception care This document includes recommendations for using specific contraceptive methods by women and men who have certain characteristics or medical conditions. Status: Current Provides recommendations to improve both preconception health and care. The goal of these recommendations is to improve the health of women and couples, before conception of a first or subsequent pregnancy. Note: Some of the recommendations have been updated/adapted in the Recommendations for HIV Prevention with Adults and Adolescents with HIV. Status: Some sections may be out of date ## Treatment, care, and viral suppression STI Treatment Guidelines (2021) Provides updated recommendations for the screening and treatment of persons who have or are at risk for sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) including HIV. Status: Current ## Prevention and care for people with HIV The guidelines and related implementation resources below provide guidance about prevention strategies to help reduce the risk of HIV transmission and improve linkage and retention in care and treatment services for people with HIV. ### Guidelines This document provides guidance to health care providers attending to the medical needs of adults and children with HIV who have been displaced from disaster areas and who have not yet secured HIV care in the areas where they have relocated. Status: Current Updates and expands the 2003 guideline, Incorporating HIV prevention into the medical care of persons living with HIV. It compiles longstanding and new federal recommendations about biomedical, behavioral, and structural interventions that can help reduce the risk of HIV transmission from persons with HIV. Status: Current This document includes recommendations for using specific contraceptive methods by women and men who have certain characteristics or medical conditions. Status: Current Provides updated recommendations for the screening and treatment of persons who have or are at risk for sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) including HIV. Status: Current Summarizes as of 2011, guidelines or recommendations published by multiple agencies of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) for prevention and control of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), and tuberculosis (TB) for persons who use drugs illicitly. Note: A few of the recommendations have been updated/adapted in the Recommendations for HIV Prevention with Adults and Adolescents with HIV (2014) and STI Treatment Guidelines. Status: Some sections may be out of date ### Implementation resources Covers resources related to this guideline. Status: Current ## Program management The document below provides guidance to professionals about methods for designing, implementing, managing, and evaluating HIV prevention, care, and treatment programs. ### Collaboration and coordination Describes the use of case management in different settings, examines benefits and barriers to case management collaboration and coordination, and identifies methods for strengthening linkages between HIV/AIDS case management programs. It includes examples of successful models to aid users in eliminating or reducing service gaps and duplication in the delivery of services. Status: Some sections may be out of date ### Implementation resources Intended to advance health equity, improve quality, and help eliminate health care disparities by establishing a blueprint for health and health care organizations. Assurance of Confidentiality Statement Status: Current This white paper outlines NCHHSTP’s strategic vision for program collaboration and service integration, building on and refining concepts outlined in a 2007 green paper. Status: Some sections may be out of date Connects learners to quality public health and healthcare training opportunities and educational tools developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), CDC partners, and other organizations recognized for developing public health training resources. Status: Current CDC TRAIN provides access to over 1300 courses developed by the CDC programs, grantees, and other funded partners. Courses offered by CDC course providers have been approved and verified by CDC. Status: Current Resources for HIV prevention providers such as health departments and community-based organizations to provide the best evidence-based HIV prevention services. Status: Current CDC-funded group of training centers created in partnership with health departments and universities. The PTCs are dedicated to increasing the knowledge and skills of health professionals in the areas of sexual health. Status: Current The TargetHIV website is the one-stop shop for technical assistance (TA) and training resources for HRSA's Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program (RWHAP), the federal program that funds local and state agencies to deliver HIV care for people with HIV who do not have full health insurance. Resources include webinars, tools, training materials, manuals, and guidelines that focus on RWHAP service delivery and agency operations. Status: Current Resource for training, education, and technical assistance to clinicians, providers and organizations in multicultural HIV/AIDS care. Status: Current Relevant guidance to help direct service-providing health departments bill third party payers. Status: Current

Free Sample Pickup at-home Free Report Counselling CAP & NABL Certified labs Presense in 250+ cities across India ## What is **HIV 1&2 Antibodies ?** An HIV test helps in the diagnosis of HIV and HIV AIDS in individuals. The test works by identifying antibodies associated with HIV 1 and HIV 2 virus. Your body releases HIV-specific antibodies when you are infected with the virus. These antibodies are your body’s defence mechanism to fight invaders; hence they are released when you are infected with the two types of HIVs. Both HIV 1 and HIV 2 are two types of HIV, but the latter develops more slowly than the former. At present, there is no cure for HIV but can be treated. HIV virus destroys the immune cells in the body, weakening your body’s defence and making you more susceptible to infections which healthy people can easily combat. HIV usually spreads through blood and sexual contact. If you come in contact with the blood of the infected person by sharing needles, or syringes or having sex with them, you can contract HIV. While HIV is the former stage, AIDS is the latter stage. Without treatment, HIV can progress into HIV AIDS wherein the body’s immunity gets impacted severely and you become prone to life-threatening infections. HIV doesn’t always display symptoms, which makes the screening tests essential if you’re a sexually active person, take drugs or are a healthcare worker exposed to needles and bloodwork. It is essential to note that both the symptoms and antibodies take time to develop, so the test may not be able to identify antibodies if you’re taking the test too soon, or immediately after coming in sexual contact with the HIV-infected person. An HIV 1 and HIV 2 antibody test may find HIV antibodies as early as 23 days after infection, but it may take as long as 90 days before your body produces enough antibodies to show up on this test. ## HIV 1 and 2 Antibody Test Preparation There is no preparation required. However, ensure you are not taking the test a bit too early. The test is accurate in identifying antibodies as early as 23 days and as late as 90 days after exposure. There are high chances of false negatives if you take the test early. ## Why Take an HIV 1 and 2 Antibody Test? An HIV test is recommended in the following instances: * **HIV 1 and HIV 2 viruses are asymptomatic in most cases. This means you may not get any symptoms even when you’re infected with the virus. Hence, this test becomes essential if you are sexually active.** * **The test is also essential if you’re a healthcare worker exposed to needles and bloodwork.** * **You take drugs via syringes.** * **You get tattoos frequently.** * **If you’re pregnant.** ## HIV 1 and 2 Antibody Test Results & Interpretation Your HIV test results will mention if you’re positive or negative for the HIV 1 and HIV 2 specific antibodies. A positive result means your blood sample had HIV antibodies. This means you’re probably infected with HIV. Your doctor will recommend a follow-up test for confirmation. In case your test results are negative, this means your blood sample didn’t have any HIV antibodies. However, it doesn’t always mean you don’t have HIV especially if you have taken the test within 90 days after possible exposure. No, they are not the same. AIDS is the later stage of HIV. If you have AIDS and you?re not getting treatment, it can progress into AIDS which can turn fatal once it makes your immune system so weak that you become prone to life-threatening infections. ### When is the right time to take the test? The time of the day doesn?t matter when you?re taking the HIV test. However, you must take the test after 90 days of the possible exposure. This is because your body needs to develop sufficient antibodies to show up on the test. 90 days and later is the best time to take the test. ### How is HIV treated? HIV is treated with antiretroviral therapy (ART), which involves taking a combination of HIV medicines every day. These medicines prevent the virus from multiplying and progressing, giving the immune system the time to repair itself. ### Can HIV be passed when someone sneezes? No. HIV is not passed on in sweat, saliva, or tears. Neither it is passed through kissing. Kissing carries a very low risk of transmission unless there are open sores in the mouth or there is blood present. ### Are there any symptoms of HIV? There may be symptoms of HIV but they can be mild enough to be neglected. These may be cold or flu which is not uncommon amongst people. These symptoms can appear 2 -4 weeks after exposure. However, more apparent symptoms can appear a decade later. ### How can treatment help if HIV is chronic? Without treatment, HIV can progress into AIDS, which destroys your immune system and affects your lifespan significantly. However, if you get treatment, the medicines prevent the multiplication of the virus and give the immune system the time to repair itself. HIV-infected persons who get treatment can expect to live almost as long as people who donot have HIV. ### Is HIV AIDS fatal? Yes. HIV AIDS can be fatal if you do not take treatment. Without treatment, patients infected with AIDS typically live for three years. ### How long will the HIV antibody take? An HIV antibody is quick. Once the phlebotomist reaches your location, it may take up to 20 minutes to collect the sample. ### Are there any food items that I must avoid? Fasting is not required for the HIV test. You can drink and eat as usual. ### Are there any medicines I am required to avoid for the HIV test? No, there is no need to pause your medications. Take them as usual and as instructed. ### Are there any other tests I need to take? Yes, further tests will be required depending on your test results and the time you took the test. Please talk to your doctor about this. ### Can alcohol and smoking affect my HIV antibody results? No, but drinking and smoking before any blood test is not recommended. ### When can I expect my HIV test reports?
